en: The second chapter states the nature of the sentence—
Locanā:

Now, in the desire to define the nature of both the sentence (*vākya*) and the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*)—the two characteristics of poetry—the author, wishing to determine the sentence, which was mentioned first, along with its auxiliary elements in the second chapter, introduces the verse that sets forth its general definition: "The nature of the sentence" (*vākyasvarūpam*).
Its own, unique form is its "nature" (*svarūpa*).
A property that distinguishes [an object] from others.

A sentence is a collection of words endowed with semantic competency (*yogyatā*), expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), and proximity (*satti*). Semantic competency is the absence of contradiction in the mutual relationship between the word-meanings.

Even in the absence of this accumulation of words (*padoccaya*), if it were still considered a sentence (*vākya*), then such expressions as "he sprinkles with fire" (*vahninā siñcati*) would also be sentences. [In response to this,] since it has been stated that poetry (*kāvyam*) is a sentence whose essence is aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), [the author] says "the nature of a sentence" (*vākyasvarūpam*) in order to state the definition of a sentence. *Vijñapriyā*: (vi, ka) Since it has been stated that poetry is a sentence whose essence is aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), he says "the nature of a sentence" (*vākyasvarūpam*) in order to state the definition of a sentence.

The absence of sublation (bādhābhāva) consists in the absence of the mere cognition of sublation; for if there were a cognition of sublation regarding the object being sublated, verbal comprehension (śābdabodha) would be impossible.
A sentence is precisely that which brings about the comprehension of a syntactic relation (anvaya), as in "He sprinkles with fire" (vahninā siñcati).

In the case of "sprinkling with fire" (*sekaṃ prati vanheḥ*), there is no comprehension of the syntactic relation (*anvaya*) because the connection of fire as the instrument (*karaṇatā*) is contradicted; therefore, no understanding of the relation arises.
Now, one might object: "In that case, should it not be stated that the very capacity to generate the comprehension of a relation is the definition [of a word]?"; [we reply:
No, for the definition is formulated by including that [capacity] in order to demonstrate the totality of conditions (*sāmagrī*) that generates the comprehension of a relation.
Expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) is the absence of the completion of comprehension;
and that consists in the listener’s desire to know.
*Vijñapriyā*:

(vi, kha) Regarding the term "desire" (*ākāṅkṣā*), he explains it as precisely the absence of the completion of comprehension, using the word "and" (*sa ca*). Furthermore, this desire for knowledge (*jijñāsā*) is an object distinct from the objects already comprehended;
it should be understood as having arisen for the purpose of subverting the connection with the objects first comprehended.
Therefore, in cases such as "the white horse," even if there is a desire to know whether it is not white due to chance, there is no *ākāṅkṣā* (expectancy).

In cases such as "Caitra’s brother goes home," the expectancy regarding Caitra’s being at home does not arise, because the cognition of the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) has already been produced with respect to the brother.
Consequently, there is no cognition [of the sentence] as "Caitra’s house."

In the case of the sentence, “The river has pure water; the buffalo roams on the bank,” although the river is presented as being possessed of pure water, because the bank is presented as its related correlate, a desire to know the bank arises for the purpose of connecting it [with the action], due to the speaker’s intention (*tātparya*) regarding the river as the related correlate. Thus, there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) in that instance.

In the case of "he sprinkles with fire" (*vahninā siñcati*), however, it should be understood that because the effect [of the instrument]—namely, the act of sprinkling—is untenable, the expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) regarding that effect necessarily arises in relation to the sprinkling.
Thus, when there is a mutually required relationship between words, compatibility (*yogyatā*) consists precisely in the absence of sublation (*bādhaviraha*);
otherwise, compatibility would absurdly follow even for "fire as an instrument" and "sprinkling," since a temporal relationship exists between them despite their lack of mutual expectancy.
Locanā:
[The syllables] "lo" and "ā" would constitute the statement;
he explains this as follows.
Regarding "fitness" (yogyatā):
regarding "of word-meanings" (padārthānām), the meanings of words such as "cow" and so forth are "word-meanings" (padārtha).

In the absence of this—namely, the absence of compatibility (yogyatā)—there is a lack of completion of the cognition even for words such as "cow" and so forth that are devoid of mutual expectancy (ākāṅkṣā). This is what [the author] clarifies by stating, "expectancy is the listener's desire to know.
Expectancy is a property of the self (ātmadharma), because, being of the nature of the listener's desire to know, it is a form of volition (icchā).
Compatibility is clearly a property of the objects (arthadharma).
Due to the absence of this [expectancy], there is no cognition of syntactic connection (*anvaya*) in cases such as "cow, horse, man, elephant.
Furthermore, even in a sentence that possesses expectancy, the designation "free from expectancy" (*nirākāṅkṣa*) occurs immediately after the cognition of syntactic connection;
thus, the absence of a verbal cognition whose form is identical to the intended cognition of syntactic connection is itself another kind of expectancy.

Therefore, the sentence "Bring the jar," having once produced a cognition of the syntactic relation (*anvayabodha*), does not produce another cognition of a syntactic relation; for there is a finality (*paryavasāna*, i.e., completion) of the cognition [once it has occurred]. (Kāvyaprakāśa-Ṭīkā-dṛṣṭi-viśvanātha)

Due to the absence (non-existence) of that [knowledge]— namely, the mere hearing of the action and the lack of understanding— the desire to know the grammatical participant (*kāraka*) [first the agent, and thereafter the object and so forth] arises spontaneously.
If being a sentence were defined merely by the absence of expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣatva*), then strings such as "cow, horse, man, elephant" would also have to be considered sentences.
*Vijñapriyā*:
[The example] "cow, horse," and so forth.

And here, precisely because there is an absence of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), even the capacity (*yogyatā*)—which consists in the absence of sublation regarding a desired connection—is non-existent; thus, due to the very absence of expectancy, there is no status as a sentence (*vākyatva*).

Furthermore, the absence of expectancy is established by the fact of our experience that no desire to know arises for the purpose of connecting the meaning of a word ending in the nominative case with another meaning of a word ending in the nominative case through a relation of difference.
In the case of non-differentiated connection (*abhedānvaya*), however, contradiction (*bādha*) itself constitutes proximity (*āsatti*), which is the non-interruption of cognition.

Even if there were an interruption of cognition, if it were still considered a single sentence, then the word *devadatta* uttered at this moment would have a syntactic connection with the word *gacchati* ("goes") uttered three days later.
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, gha) He states the definition of proximity (*āsatti*): the meaning is that when the cognition of one word follows immediately after the cognition of another word, there is proximity between them. And this "immediacy" [is defined] as being uninterrupted by any other meaningful word whose referent is not useful for the connection with that [word].
Or, [the meaning] may be understood after a long time;

for by means of the wood, there is the utility of its connection with objects such as the cooking pot. However, when there is an intervention by something meaningless, there is indeed non-proximity—as in the case of “sa vai gacchati,” where the particle *vai*, although meaningless, must be understood as being employed solely because it is used by authoritative persons.
But this does not refer to particles such as *ca* (and) and so forth.

Therefore, the meaning [of proximity] is non-intervention by that which has a sense not useful for the connection with that [word], or by that which is meaningless and not employed by authoritative persons (*prāmāṇika*).
However, in the case of "The mountain possesses fire because Devadatta ate," there is no proximity between the words "mountain" (*giri*) and "possessing fire" (*agnimat*).
Because it is separated by the words "following that" (tadanvaya), "unused," and "eaten";
whereas in the case of separation by time, the length of that time consists precisely in its being the locus for the interruption of the stream of cognitions regarding those words.

In this regard, he demonstrates the absence of non-existence [of the definition] with the words "even upon the cessation of cognition. It should not be argued that if the memory of the meanings of the previously uttered words exists there, then for that very reason the status of being a sentence (*vākyatva*) applies;
nor should it be said that the absence of the status of being a sentence follows simply from the non-arising of verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*) due to that [memory] being absent.

This is because the capacity to generate verbal comprehension is not included in the definition of non-existence; therefore, it is precisely appropriate to demonstrate the over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of the definition to such a sentence, since it fails to generate verbal comprehension due to the absence of the memory of those words.

In this context, although expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and compatibility (*yogyatā*) reside in the self and the meaning [respectively], they are figuratively attributed to the collection of words (*padoccaya*).
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, ṅa) But surely, since compatibility—which consists in the absence of subverting cognition—and expectancy—which consists in the desire to know—reside in the self and the meaning?

To the question, "How is the collection of words (*padoccaya*) connected with that [absence of contradiction]? he says: "Of expectancy and compatibility. "Metaphorical application" (*upacāra*) is a function (*vṛtti*) by way of the relation of being an object (*viṣayatā-sambandha*).

And that [function] belongs directly to the collection of words—which is the object of the absence of contradiction—since the counter-positive of that absence, namely the cognition of contradiction, has that very collection as its object.
A collection of sentences is a "great sentence" (*mahāvākya*).
"Endowed with fitness, expectancy, and proximity"—thus is a sentence considered to be of two kinds. (VisSd 2.1)
"In this manner" means as a sentence and as a great sentence (*mahāvākya*).
And it is stated in the *Tantravārttika*:
"For those [sentences] which are complete in the communication of their own meaning, there arises a mutual dependence based on the relationship of subordinate and principal."
Furthermore, the unity of multiple sentences arises through their combination.
Thus [ends the citation].
Locanā:
With "lo, i," she demonstrates that even a great sentence (*mahāvākya*) constitutes poetry by showing the consensus of the masters, stating: "As it has been said."

In literary compositions (*prabandhas*), even sentences that are fragmented may function as related members (*aṅga-aṅgin*) through their mutual relationship; however, without this relationship of member and principal, they would fall into incoherence, like the ravings of a madman.
The logical connection (*anvaya*) is that, in cases such as "by combining" or "assembling" sentences and great sentences (*vākya-mahāvākya*), there is a distinct exclusion for each individual part.
Multiple words are mutually expectant,
as in "Devadatta [drives] the cow with a staff.
Furthermore, multiple sentences are well-known in literary compositions to be dependent upon one another for the sake of awakening the understanding of a unified meaning through their combination.
For in the opinion of Bhaṭṭa, the capacity of such words and sentences lies only in conveying multiple distinct meanings separately, and not in conveying a single unified meaning.
An example of such a sentence is: “The bedchamber was empty,” and so forth (p. 22).
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, ca) He states the twofold nature of a sentence: "a collection of sentences.

Since there is a requirement for both—because in some cases it is the mere sentence and in others it is the great sentence (mahāvākya)—that they be considered as such when defining them, he says, "compatibility, expectancy," etc., indicating that even in the definition of the great sentence, compatibility and the like serve as qualifiers.

In that context, regarding the sentence "The fire burns on wet wood; he sprinkles it with water," because this would result in the status of being a *mahāvākya* (a complex sentence), in order to prevent that, [the requirement of] semantic compatibility (*yogyatā*) is specified. [For example:
"Caitra cooks;
Maitra goes."

This is for the purpose of excluding [the definition from applying to] two sentences uttered on different days; and the inclusion of "expectancy" (*ākāṅkṣā*) is for the purpose of excluding two mutually contradictory sentences that are separated by other sentences, as well as two expectant and compatible sentences [that lack proximity].

In the example beginning with "The bedchamber is empty," since all the word-meanings are expectant of what follows, there is no completion of the cognition of any individual meaning, and thus it does not constitute a "great sentence" (*mahāvākya*).
A great sentence (*mahāvākya*) is, for example, the *Rāmāyaṇa*, the *Mahābhārata*, the *Raghuvaṃśa*, and so forth;
it has been stated that a collection of words constitutes a sentence.

In this regard, what is the definition of a word (*pada*)? To this he says: "Letters (*varṇa*), when capable of being used and conveying a single meaning that is not [already] connected [to another], constitute a word."—*Vijñapriyā*.
(vi, cha) — Regarding the definition "phonemes constitute a word": this is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning that they are both "fit for usage" and "conveying a single non-composite meaning.
In the phrase "conveying a single meaning," the sense is "conveying each individual meaning.
By this, there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) in the case of words within a sentence that convey multiple meanings through their combination.
For "possessing a single meaning" means having as many meanings as there are words themselves;
this is because it is impossible to speak of a single meaning [when multiple meanings are present].

It should not be argued that there is an over-narrow application (*avyāpti*) of the definition in the case of the expression "three kinds of liquor" (*na trividhā surā*), because the single word *surā* there conveys all three—Gauḍī, Paiṣṭhī, and Mādhvī.

In that context, regarding the acceptance of the understanding of the connection through the repetition "gauḍī surā, paiṣṭhī surā, mādhvī surā," there is no lack of pervasion (avyāpti), because the three occurrences of the word *surā* convey meanings equal in number to themselves.

Nor should it be argued that there is a lack of pervasion in the case of "Taitra-Maitra-Devadattāḥ sundarāḥ" (Taitra, Maitra, and Devadatta are handsome), because the single word *sundara* does not convey a triad of handsome persons; for the term *artha* (meaning) refers to the delimitors of the meaning (*arthatāvacchedaka*), and thus beauty is indeed one.

Nor should it be said that there is still an over-narrow definition (*avyāpti*) in the case of "the three kinds of liquor" (*trividhā surā*), because when there is more than one delimitor of the meaning (*arthatāvacchedaka*), repetition (*āvṛtti*) itself is accepted [of the suffix].
For example: *ghaṭaḥ*.
This excludes the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) from being the locus of application.
Vijñapriyā:
Regarding the term "of the nominal stem" (*pratipadikasya*), the meaning is "belonging to that alone.
This is because only that which ends in a case-suffix is accepted as being a *pada*.
For a bare nominal stem is not fit for usage without a case-ending;

nor should it be argued that a word whose single meaning is not syntactically connected cannot function as a word, because according to the theory of Abhihitānvaya (the expression of meanings followed by their connection), such a word simply does not express a [syntactically] connected meaning.
"In 'ananvitā' [refers] to sentences and great sentences.
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, jha):
The connection is with "exclusion" (*vyavaccheda*) in the phrase "of sentences and great sentences."
This is precisely because those two [words] convey a meaning that is mutually related (*anvitārtha*).

Here, although the exclusion of a sentence—which conveys multiple meanings—is possible simply by virtue of its conveying a single meaning, it should be noted that the inclusion of that qualification is intended solely to indicate our intention: "We do not favor the theory of the expression of the related (*anvitābhidhānavāda*)."
"Of those consisting of multiple words that are expectant" (*sākāṅkṣānekapada*) means:
the exclusion of such sentences in which there are multiple words that are expectant (*sākāṅkṣa*). This is the meaning.
And here, it is precisely "of sentences" (*vākyānām*) that is intended;
for by the very fact of being a sentence, both the state of having multiple words and mutual expectancy are already established.
Their mention [in the definition] is solely for the purpose of explaining the essential nature [of a sentence].
Nor should it be argued that the exclusion of sentences that convey unconnected meanings follows solely from the qualification "conveying connected meanings";
for the statement "of sentences" (*vākyānām*) is intended precisely to prevent two sentences whose meanings are mutually connected from collectively attaining the status of a single word (*padatva*).
By the phrase "unconnected meanings," etc., however, only each individual sentence is excluded.
"Those which convey meaning" refers to [sounds] such as *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, and *pa*.
In the term "phonemes" (*varṇāḥ*), the plural number is not intended to be significant.
*Vijñapriyā*:

Regarding the phrase "of *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, *pa*, etc."— now, in the expression "fit for usage" (*prayogārha*), "usage" does not mean mere utterance, for if it did, there would be the undesirable consequence of excluding nominal stems (*pratipadika*). Rather, what must necessarily be stated is that utterance is for the purpose of conveying meaning.
If it is argued that since the mere nominal stem (*pratipadika*) is not uttered for that purpose [of conveying meaning],
and thus the exclusion of meaningless sounds such as *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, and *ta* follows naturally from the very word suitable for usage, this is true.
However, in the absence of the requirement of "conveying meaning," the non-inclusion of the qualifier "meaningless" (*ananvita*) results simply from a lack of necessity.

Furthermore, since there would otherwise be the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to both simple sentences and great sentences (*mahāvākya*) when that [qualification] is not included, and because there is no possibility of avoiding this by adding the term "non-connected" (*ananvita*), one must—conforming to that requirement—adopt the qualification of "being expressive of a specific meaning.

This is precisely why the intention is to exclude such cases as *ka-ca-ṭa-ta-pi* and so forth. Regarding the phrase "the letters *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, *pa*, etc., are parts of words," he states "letters" (*varṇāḥ*) to indicate that plurality is not intended.
Locanā:

Regarding the phrase "the letters" (*varṇāḥ*), the plural number is not intended to be significant; therefore, it includes both a single letter and two letters as well. Thus, in the phrase "may you be gracious toward me," there is the inclusion of the single letter *a*, which is stated to be related to Vāsudeva.
There is no loss of the status of being a word (*padatva*).
"In that regard" means: as far as possible, in both words and sentences.
Meaning (*artha*) is considered to be threefold: the expressed (*vācya*), the indicated (*lakṣya*), and the suggested (*vyaṅgya*).
He states their essential nature:

"The meaning to be expressed is understood through denotation (*abhidhā*); that which is indicated is considered [understood] through indication (*lakṣaṇā*); and that which is suggested is [understood] through suggestion (*vyañjanā*). These are the three powers of a word. (VisSd 2.3)
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ṭha) Since fitness (*yogyatā*) and expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) are constituted by the object (*artha*), he states the divisions of the object with the words "the object," etc.
Its own nature (*svarūpa*) is its definition (*lakṣaṇa*).
The powers (*śaktayaḥ*) are the functions (*vṛttayaḥ*).
Locanā:

(lo, u) In that regard, according to the view of those who maintain that the meaning is expressed through the connection (*abhihitānvayavādinaḥ*), it will be stated that even the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) is denotable by the words.
And in the view of those who maintain that meaning is denoted by the sentence (*vākya*), the meaning of a single word is both denotable (*abhidheya*) and indicated (*lakṣya*),
while it is suggested (*vyaṅgya*) by letters, words, sentences, and so forth.

As for those who maintain that [functions] such as *anvita* (relatedness) and so forth reside in the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) as seen in actual usage (*lakṣya*), in their view it is only the exclusion of that [literal meaning] (*tatparyyāvṛtti*) which conveys the sentence-meaning;
this is another name for the second type of indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

Now, one might object: in cases such as "The hamlet is on the Ganges" (*gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*), it is the function of indication (*lakṣaṇā*)—to be described later—that conveys the meaning of the bank (*taṭa*).
Since the secondary (gauṇī) function must be included within indication (lakṣaṇā), the secondary meaning is not mentioned separately.

Here, because the discussion concerns the concomitance of denotation (abhidhā) and indication (lakṣaṇā) with suggestion (vyañjanā), the statement that [suggestion] consists solely of the power of the word is merely illustrative. In the context of suggestion and indication, however, according to the view of Bhaṭṭa, it is said: "That function called suggestion belongs to the word as well as to the meaning and so forth."
Thus he will say:
"Those [functions] beginning with denotation (abhidhā). Among them, the first is denotation (abhidhā), because it brings about the understanding of a conventionalized meaning.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ḍa) Regarding that, he states the definition of denotation (*abhidhā*): "In that context, of the conventionalized meaning...
The definition is precisely the etymological sense (*yogārtha*): *abhidhā* means that which is denoted or made understood.
Regarding the question of what meaning is understood there such that the etymological sense (*yogārtha*) is of that nature, he says: "conventional" (*saṃketita*).
Conventional usage (*vṛtti*) is not denotation (*abhidhā*), because that would result in the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*).
Therefore, that [suffix] was employed for the purpose of grasping;
in this context, by means of the *kta* suffix, the meaning is "of that which has already grasped its own function.
Thus, it must be explained how *vyañjanā* (suggestion), which makes known meanings whose functions have not yet been grasped, is excluded.

Since the word would be grasped as having that secondary function (vṛtti) by implication, there would consequently be an over-extension (ativyāpti) of the definition; therefore, he says "agnim eti" (he goes to the fire).
This means "grasped first.
For a secondary function (lakṣaṇā), however, is grasped only after the primary power (śakti) has been apprehended and an obstacle (bādhā) to its application has arisen.
For this very reason, he will explain [it later] as "not separated by another power" (śaktyantarānantaritā).
However, some explain the meaning of the word *agrimā* (the subsequent) as referring to the three functions (*vṛtti*) mentioned previously;
that is not correct.

For otherwise, by expressing it through that [indirect] manner, there would result the fallacy of *ananvaya* (lack of syntactic connection); furthermore, the interpretation that [the meaning] is "not mediated by another power" (*śaktyantara-anantarita*) would be untenable.

When an elder says to a middle-aged person, "Bring the cow," and the latter is observed to proceed toward bringing the cow, the child [perceives] that the meaning of this sentence is "the bringing of a body possessing a dewlap and so forth."

Thus one first understands [the general meaning]; immediately thereafter, through the process of insertion and deletion in such instances as "Bind the cow" and "Bring the horse," one determines the convention that the word *go* has the meaning "that which possesses a dewlap and so forth," and the word *ānayana* has the meaning "bringing."—
Vijñapriyā.
(vi, ḍha) In that regard, the grasping of convention is for the purpose of observing the usage of elders;
he demonstrates that manner [of usage] with the words "the superior," etc. Relying on a particular view, he explains: "the superior," etc.
The middle [person] is the elder;
the child is the one desiring to learn.
This means "of an indivisible sentence."

The meaning of the sentence as a whole is the bringing of a lump [of matter] possessing a dewlap and so forth; however, one does not understand— that is, one does not know— that "go" refers individually to that which possesses a dewlap and so forth, nor that "bringing" means fetching.
"Of this sentence":
by this, the initial apprehension of the capacity (*śaktigraha*) between the sentence and its meaning is shown;
*āvāpa* is the proposition (*pratijñā*).
*Udvāpa* means extraction (*uddhāra*). *Āvāpa* and *udvāpa* refer to the removal of a heard word and the hearing of another word in its place. — *Locanā*:

(lo, ū) He states the nature of denotation (*abhidhā*) and the other [functions] in sequence. Regarding that, this is the meaning of the verse concerning *anvitābhidhāna*: for those who have already acquired proficiency (*vyutpanna*) in the relationship between word and its referent as signifier (*vācaka*) and signified (*vācya*), there is the comprehension of the sentence-meaning;
and proficiency arises only from the usage of elders, and that [usage] consists solely of sentences.
And a sentence is necessarily restricted to the cognition of a related [meaning].
Consequently, at the time of instruction, the apprehension of the relationship occurs only with respect to that which is already related.

Now, one might ask: "In that case, how is there a comprehension of meaning in the case of words—which are parts of a sentence—and in the case of words situated within different sentences, apart from the cognition of word-meanings? To this, he says: "And immediately thereafter..."
This is the intended meaning: although every acquisition of linguistic proficiency is preceded by the usage of elders, and that usage of elders occurs solely through sentences,
nevertheless, for the cognition of whichever constituent word-form within a sentence, there is the insertion of whichever constituent meaning.

When a word is excluded upon the exclusion of a certain object, the expressive power (*śakti*) of that word for that object is understood through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), as it is supported by the very observation of insertion (*āvāpa*) and exclusion (*uddhāra*).
Thus, in this view, it is indicated that the apprehension of convention (*saṃketagraha*) occurs through the means of knowledge consisting of inference of the suffix and presumptive testimony.
As they say:
"In this context, one perceives through direct perception the word, the elder, and the object denoted;
and one perceives the listener's comprehension through inference based on their behavior."
And by means of *anyathānupapatti* (the impossibility otherwise), one should understand the capacity for cognition as being twofold;
and by means of *arthāpatti* (presumption), one should understand the relationship [between word and meaning] as being established by three means of valid cognition (*tripramāṇaka*).”
Thus;
for its meaning is as follows: "word" refers to a sentence such as "bring the cow," and "the elders" refers to the instigator and the one being instigated.
The denotable object consists of the bringing of the cow and so forth.

The listener perceives and knows these through direct perception. Furthermore, the body and the inference [are as follows]: this activity of the elder directed by the instigator is preceded by a cognition corresponding to that [activity].
Because it is an activity,
like my own activity of such a kind;
and that activity is produced by this particular application.

Because it conforms to this positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), one understands— by means of *anyathānupapatti* (the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the fact)— that the capacity consisting of the relationship between signifier and signified belongs to that whose nature (*svarūpa*) is the self; namely, the restriction of the signifying function to the sentence as the substratum (*āśraya*) and the restriction of the signified function to the object (*viṣaya*), which is established through the activity of the elder who prompts the action.
[Objection: "In that case, because of the connection with distinct sentences, the acquisition of linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*) would have to be observed for every single sentence;
and since that is difficult to establish, there would be a cessation of verbal communication. To this, he says: "And by means of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).
Here, by the word "and" (*ca*), there is a reference back to the phrase "the power [of words] consists of two natures regarding cognition."
In the reading "avabudhyate" (he understands), however, that [word] refers back to it by its very meaning.
And thus the sense is this:

through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) aided by the observation of the process of extraction and insertion (*āpoddhāra*), he knows the capacity—which consists of those two meanings and is connected as signifier and signified—belonging to the form of the word-part whose conventional relationship has been grasped.

As for *arthāpatti* (presumption), it consists of two types: one is the cognition of the relationship between a sentence and its meaning as that of the signifier and the signified (*vācya-vācaka*), and the other is the cognition of the relationship between a word and its meaning; these two types of *arthāpatti* are generally counted as one. Furthermore, in some cases, [it arises] from the co-occurrence with a well-known word, as for example:
In the case of [the cognition] "here the bee drinks honey within the interior of a blooming lotus," it arises from some instance of authoritative instruction, as for example:
"this is what is denoted by the word 'horse'."
Vijñapriyā:
(lo, ṛ) In some cases, he shows the apprehension of a convention through a single instance of comparison or means of valid cognition—this is expressed by the words "in some cases" (*kvacit*).
The meaning is this: the establishment of the means of valid cognition known as comparison (*upamāna*) is indeed threefold.
As they say: “Similarity is merely a property, and dissimilarity is [also] a property by virtue of difference”;
therein, similarity is as in "the gavaya is similar to a cow," and dissimilarity is as in "the cuckoo is dissimilar to a crow."
The subject under discussion is merely the property (*dharma*).

An example of the "to-be-adopted" (*upādeya*) and so forth follows: here, through the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with words well-known for having previously established conventions that convey the property of being a drinker of honey within the interior of a blooming lotus, the referent of the word *madhukara* is the bee.

Thus he grasps the convention (*saṅketa*). And this is an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*); by it, the apprehension of conventions through the means of valid cognition of comparison (*upamāna*)—as in "the *gavaya* is similar to a cow" and "the *kokila* is dissimilar to a crow"—is indicated. Since in some cases [the convention is grasped] through the means of valid cognition of verbal testimony (*śabda*), he says: "in some cases."
A trustworthy person is one who is reliable and whose words are determined to be true;
therefore, even when told "this is what is denoted by the word 'horse'," one grasps the convention regarding the object that is a horse.
And making that conventional meaning understood, the power of the word is not mediated by any other power;
this is the meaning of the term "unmediated by another power" (*śaktyantarānantarita*) in the first verse-quarter of the *Vijñapriyā*.
By this, the reversal between indication (*lakṣaṇā*) and suggestion (*vyañjanā*) is indicated.
For indication is indeed always mediated by denotation (*abhidhā*);
whereas suggestion, where indication is absent, is not mediated by denotation.
That [non-duality] is mediated by a second,
or rather,

by what is called "subsequent"; for just as Caitra and others are designated by their respective names, so too is that [non-duality] characterized by non-duality as mediated by a convention, even when it is the object of a name such as "Caitra" which has been previously mentioned as the mode of its being dependent.
It has been indicated that "power" (śakti) is what is called "denotation" (abhidhā).
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, ṇa) "In some cases" (*kvacit*)—this refers to co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*), which is the mention [of a word] within a single sentence as being connected [to another].
Regarding the term "distinct" (*prabhinnā*): here, the words *madhu* ("honey") and *pibati* ("drinks") are well-known.

Even for someone who has not yet grasped the conventional power (*śakti*) of the word *madhukara* ("bee"), the power of that word is grasped with respect to the bee, because it is connected to the drinking of honey mentioned in co-occurrence.
"And that which is conventionalized" (saṅketita) means that its function has been grasped by various perceivers.
"Not separated from another power" (śaktyantarānantarita) means that its functional operation is not interrupted by the apprehension of that [other] power.
This is the explanation of the subsequent word.
The conventional designation is apprehended in respect to a genus, as well as in respect to qualities, substances, and actions.
A genus (*jāti*) is [the universal] such as "cowness" (*gotva*) in individual cows and the like.
A quality (*guṇa*) is an established property of a real entity that is the cause for conferring a specific distinction;
for qualities such as "white" differentiate a cow and the like from those of the same class that are black and so forth.
Substance-words (*dravyaśabda*) are those that denote a single individual, such as *hari*, *hara*, *ḍittha*, *ḍavittha*, and so forth.
Actions (*kriyā*) are properties of things (*vastudharma*) whose nature is to be accomplished (*sādhyarūpa*), such as cooking (*pāka*) and the like.

For in these cases, the collection of operations (*vyāpārakalāpa*) consisting of a sequence of prior and posterior stages, beginning with placing [the pot] on the fire and ending with taking it off, is what is denoted by words such as "cooking."

For it is precisely in these limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the individuals that the convention is grasped, and not in the individuals themselves, because that would entail the faults of infinite regress and deviation (*ānantya-vyabhicāra*).
*Vijñapriyā*:

(Vi, Ta) Now, one might ask: "Is the conventionally designated object a property (*dharma*) or the possessor of properties (*dharmin*)? To this he replies: "The conventionally designated... According to the sequence already stated, the objects that are the referents of the grasping of conventions differ according to the difference in words. "Bestowing a distinction" means generating the cognition of a difference from others.

He says that whatever property of a thing has this nature is established as eternal—"the property of the thing is established"—and these qualities (*guṇas*) are likewise indeed eternal. However, the perception of their arising and destruction is merely in the form of manifestation and disappearance;

it causes one to grasp the imposition of specific distinctions among the qualities—as in "white" and so forth—since they differentiate and make known [objects] through their distinct characteristics, as in "Hari" and "Hara.
And this is said provided that a difference in individuals is not admitted due to the differences in states such as childhood and so on.
However, in the view of those who accept that [position], even this is indeed a genus-term (*jāti-śabda*).
It should be understood that words such as "ether" (*ākāśa*), "Vindhya," and "Mandara" denote individual substances (*vyakti-dravya*).

As for "action" (*kriyā*)—being of the nature of something to be accomplished (*sādhya-rūpa*) and produced (*janya-rūpa*)—action lacks eternality because even atoms (*paramāṇu*) are devoid of action during the great dissolution (*mahā-pralaya*).
Therefore, since that [color] is produced, there is the conceptualization of its manifestation and disappearance.

As for the colors not produced by heat (*apākaja-rūpa*), they reside in atoms and are indeed eternal; thus, the intention is that eternity—defined as the property of being the locus of the categories residing therein—belongs to all qualities.

"In these alone" means that among these properties of substances in the form of actions which are to be understood, the term "cooking" (*pāka*) and so forth denotes the entire complex of actions beginning with placing [the pot] on the fire and ending with removing it from the fire.
The point is this: otherwise, in the case of cooking—which is constituted by multiple actions—what would be the meaning of the verbal root (the action denoted by the verb)?
"In these alone" means: in these limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*s) [such as cowness], which exist without the substance (*dravya*).
"Due to infinity" means: because it is impossible to grasp the word-potency (*śakti*) in every instance there, owing to the infinity of individual cows and so forth.

And if it is argued that the apprehension of the convention (*saṃketa*) occurs with respect to only a single individual, he says: "deviation" (*vyabhicāra*). The meaning is this: even in an individual distinct from that one in which the convention was apprehended, but belonging to the same class, there arises the cognition of the effect—even without the apprehension of the capacity (*śakti*)—due to the awakening of its own nature; thus, there is the acceptance of deviation.
*Locanā*.
(lo, ḷ) Here, some say that the meaning of a word is the genus (*jāti*) alone; others [say] it is both the genus and the individual (*vyakti*).

Having set aside other views such as those of Vyāḍi, who held that [words denote] the individual, the form, and the genus, [the author] states "convention" (saṅketa), relying on the opinion of the author of the Mahābhāṣya; for all verbal compositions are rooted in grammar, and in treatises on poetics, usage generally follows that very principle.
He explains the category of quality (guṇapadārtha) by saying "quality" (guṇa).

The phrase "the cause of producing a distinction" excludes *jāti* (universal); "established" excludes *kriyā* (action). He states the justification for qualities being the cause of producing a distinction: "white and so forth."
Cows and the like possess the fitness for the linguistic usage "cow" by virtue of their genus (*jāti*).
Regarding the phrase "as a substance," etc.:

even without a [general] cause, this [term] is applied to specific individuals through the speaker’s convention in the form of "This is Ḍittha" or "This is Ḍavittha," by way of pointing them out individually (*śṛṅgagrāhikayā*).
A word that brings about the cognition of an object such as "Dittha" within a void of its own genus is the object of convention (*saṃketa*).
It exists as a sequence of prior and posterior [moments], forming a continuum through the relationship of cause and effect by way of being constituent parts of the primary action.
"In these very [factors]" means: in these [categories] such as genus (*jāti*) and so forth.

And here, although it is impossible for the substance itself to be the object of a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), its reality [is established] through metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) by virtue of the name being the adjunct. Furthermore, in the case of names such as "Dittha," since there is no infinite regress or deviation, the apprehension of the convention regarding the relationship between the signifier and the signified is possible even without an adjunct; thus, an adjunct is not required.
Moreover, if one were to admit an adjunct in the operation of a name-word conceived according to the speaker's own will, there would be the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*).
Nevertheless, the status of the notion of "substance" (*dravya-saṃjñā*) as a limiting condition (*upādhi*) has been stated in accordance with common cognition.

For this very reason, it was said that [the term applies] "to qualities, substances, and actions," or "to substances and actions," because in those cases there is no occurrence of the faults of infinite regress (*anantya*) or over-extension (*vyabhicāra*).
Because individuals are infinite and because each possesses a distinct configuration of lines, sub-lines, and so forth, it is impossible to grasp them all together.

[Objection: But if this is so, since the word "cow" and others are conventionally established (*saṃketita*) with reference to the universal (*jāti*), how can there be a cognition of the individual when that universal has vanished?
For without the recollection of an invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*), there can be no implication (*ākṣepa*).

Or, just as the consideration of the inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) of fire and the like residing in smoke and so forth is here sublated by non-perception (*anupalabdhi*); since the individual (*vyakti*) is useless in that regard, it cannot enter into the verbal synthesis (*śābda-anvaya*) without being conveyed by the word. Therefore, the secret is this: when a word denotes a universal (*jāti*), it is appropriate to rely on *vyañjanā* alone as its function in order to convey that [individual].
And thus, there is no dispute regarding the position that [words] denote the mere genus (*jāti*) as a convention.
Furthermore, the words employed for the purpose of dispelling doubt do not directly signify the individual form (*vyakti-rūpa*), which is the primary constituent of the relation;
rather, they signify only the universal (*sāmānya*), which serves as its external adjunct.
This is inconsistent.

For even those who say, "The convention [of a word] applies only to a universal (jāti) that is concomitant with an individual," must admit that the universal under discussion is itself unconventional; and since there would be an absence of any conventionalized particulars, [their position is untenable].
In order for there to be the cognition of an individual capable of connection with the primary meaning, another power (śakti) must necessarily be admitted.
Since it is accepted that a universal (sāmānya) is related to all its particulars, if every particular were known through convention (saṅketa), it would follow that everyone would be omniscient.

However, at the time of the initial instruction, because all individuals are present before one, they are accepted as being characterized by the universal; thus, even for a modern person, the specific individual (svalakṣaṇa) is [cognized] just as it was at the time of the first teaching.
Cognition would occur through direct presence alone;
therefore, since there is a direct cognition that establishes the positive concomitance (*anvaya*), what could be the seed for the word’s function without another power? Enough of this prolixity.
Now, as for indication (*lakṣaṇā*)—

When the primary meaning is sublated, that power by which another meaning connected to it is understood—whether through conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) or for a specific purpose (*prayojana*)—is the conferred capacity known as indication (*lakṣaṇā*). 2.5.
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, tha) Since it has been stated that "that which is to be indicated" (*lakṣya*) is to be grasped through indication (*lakṣaṇā*), he states the definition of indication: "the primary meaning" (*mukhyārtha*), etc.
The primary meaning is the denotable meaning (*śakyārtha*).
In this context, the meaning is: "when the sublation of the connection of the other word-meaning is known.

For instance, in the case of "a hamlet on the Gaṅgā" (*gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*), there is no sublation of the primary meaning of the Gaṅgā itself; rather, there is only a sublation of the connection of the other word-meaning, namely the hamlet.
"Connected with that" means connected with the primary meaning; "another" means other than the primary meaning.
The phrase "by means of the function [of the word] being known" is to be supplied as the remainder.
That cognition is not dependent solely upon the cognition of the sublation of the primary meaning.
Rather, it is [used] either by convention (*rūḍhi*) or for a specific purpose (*prayojana*).
Convention is usage over a long period of time.

Thus, that function (*vṛtti*)—made known by these three [factors]—by which a meaning other than the primary meaning, yet connected to the primary meaning, is understood, is "power" (*śakti*); the sense is that this function is "indication" (*lakṣaṇā*).

And that [suggestion] is "produced" by the speaker as having the indicated meaning (lakṣyārtha) as its object— this is the sense; and thus it should be understood as consisting solely of the speaker's intention (tātparya),
and not as the form of a relation between the primary meaning and the secondary meaning (śakyasambandha) as stated by the Naiyāyikas.
This is because that [sentence-meaning] cannot be assigned by any other [function].

As for the function called *tātparya* (intentionality) regarding the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgyārtha*) which was stated by the author of the *Dhvanyāloka*, and the function called *tātparya* regarding the connection between two word-meanings (*padārtha*) which was stated by the ancient Naiyāyikas—that is not indicated by these three [functions];
therefore, it is indeed distinct from them.

Even when there is a cognition of the connection of another word-meaning with the primary meaning, there is simply the impossibility of cognizing the intended connection—which is the object of the speaker's intention—in the form of the delimitor of primacy (*mukhyatāvacchedaka*).

Consequently, in cases such as "The umbrella-bearers go" (*chatriṇo gacchanti*) and "The spears enter" (*kuntāḥ praviśanti*), although there exists a connection between the primary meanings—the umbrella-bearers and the spears—with the acts of going and entering, there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) because the aforementioned sublation of the primary meaning is present.

This is because the intended connection, in its specific forms as "being a leader of a group of umbrella-bearers" and "being a spear," cannot be established through the delimitors of primacy, namely "umbrella-bearing-ness" (*chattritva*) and "spear-ness" (*kuntatva*).

Furthermore, if the status of being the intended object (*tātparyaviṣayatva*) were not included [in the definition], then because the connection of "going" in the case of the umbrella-bearer (*chattrin*) and the connection of "entering" in the case of the spear-bearer (*kuntin*) would arise through the primary delimiters (*mukhyatāvacchedaka*) of "umbrella-bearing-ness" (*chattritva*) and "spear-bearing-ness" (*kuntatva*), there would be the consequence of under-extension (*avyāpti*) in those cases.
Likewise, if the phrase "by way of the form that is the primary delimiter" were not included, there would likewise be under-extension in those very two cases;

for the connection of "going" with the umbrella-bearer and caravan-leader who is the intended object, and the connection of "entering" with the spear-bearer, are established by the delimiters of the secondary signification (*lakṣatāvacchedaka*), namely "being an umbrella-bearer and caravan-leader" and "being a spear-bearer."
In the expression "different from the primary meaning" (*anyo'rthaḥ*), the sense is "delimited by a property other than that which delimits the primary status.

Consequently, even when the word *ghaṭa* has a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for a blue pot, there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*), because although that [blue pot] lacks the state of being different from a pot,
it is delimited by "being a blue pot," which is a property other than the delimitor of primary status, namely "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*).
Locanā:

(lo, e) "Now" (*atha*)—that is to say, immediately following the mention [of the previous topic], the indication (*lakṣaṇā*), which has reached its turn according to the sequence of the enumeration of definitions, is now being examined; this is the remainder [of the sentence].

Regarding "the primary meaning" (*mukhyārtha*): the primary meaning of words such as "Ganges" is that which consists of water and so forth; and when there is an impossibility of that [primary meaning] connecting with another entity to be contained [within it], [indication occurs].

Nor is it the case that just anything whatsoever is perceived as being the very same thing [as the primary meaning], for that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*); therefore, he says: "connected with that" (*tadyukta*).

By whatever connection—whether by way of proximity or otherwise—that other object, such as the riverbank (*taṭa*), is perceived or understood through the power of the word (*śabdaśakti*) associated with that primary sense;

yet, the perception of the indicated meaning (*lakṣyārtha*) does not arise from mere connection alone, as that too would lead to an over-extension; thus he says: "through convention (*rūḍhi*) or through a purpose (*prayojana*)."

In some cases, it is due to conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), which is established through the linguistic practice of ancient elders; in other cases, it is for the purpose of indicating an excellence such as sanctity (*pāvanatva*).
Furthermore, the transferred meaning (*arpitapadārtha*) is quite evident within the very function (*vṛtti*) itself.
Thus, in this instance of indication (*lakṣaṇā*), there are three causes, the first being the sublation of the primary meaning (*mukhyārthabādha*).
And that relation [of the word to its meaning] consists in being conventional in some cases and based on a specific purpose in others.
For instance, in expressions such as "Kaliṅga is a violent man," the word *kaliṅga* refers to its own primary meaning in the form of a particular region and so forth.
That power of a word by which, being impossible [in its primary sense], it causes one to understand persons and so forth connected with itself;

and that by which, in cases such as "a hamlet on the Gaṅgā," a word like "Gaṅgā"—being impossible in its current context because it denotes an object consisting of water and the like—denotes its bank and so forth through a relationship such as proximity:
that power of the word, which is other than its natural [primary] power and is either bestowed [by convention] or manifested by God, is called *lakṣaṇā* (indication).
In the former case, the cause is *rūḍhi*, which is simply conventional usage.

In the latter case, the purpose (*prayojana*) consists in making known the excellence of coolness and purity, which is obtained through the understanding of the expression "the hamlet on the bank of the Gaṅgā.

It has been stated that, otherwise, there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), whereby anything whatsoever related [to the primary sense] could be indicated even without a specific cause.
“‘This [term] arises either from conventional usage (rūḍhi) or from a specific purpose (prayojana).
Vijñapriyā (vi, da) explains: “In the case of ‘Kaliṅga’...”
Regarding the phrase "other than the inherent" (*svābhāviketara*): the inherent function of words such as *go* (cow) is their power (*śakti*), which is distinct from that [other function].
Although it is inherent, he says "other than" because of the faults of tautology and prolixity; the meaning is "that which is regulated by the Lord alone."

Even if there were no intention on the part of the speaker because [the word] is produced from the womb of the *mātr̥kā*, it is impossible for that [intention] to be distinct from God, since it is governed by God.
However, in the view of the Mīmāṃsakas who do not accept God, the meaning is that it is "other" than any other ontological category distinct from the form of power (*śakti*).
Power (*śakti*) is the function (*vṛtti*).
"Previously" means in the passage "Kaliṅga is [called] Sāhaska.
"Fame" (prasiddhi) means usage over a vast period of time.
"Over-extension" (atiprasaṅga) refers to the fact that this particular indication (lakṣaṇā), which is fit for the usage of poets, is now being explained.
Indication (lakṣaṇā) that is devoid of conventional usage or purpose will be described as "interpretable meaning" (neyārtha),
and it is indeed a defect in poetry.
The meaning is that there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in that case.
Locanā:
(lo, ai) Having first shown an example, she clarifies the meaning of the verse through the commentary, beginning with "Kaliṅga."

He asks: "Why is the usage [of the word] unestablished when its own primary meaning is intended?"—because the meaning in the form of a specific place and so forth, being insentient, cannot logically connect with meanings such as "rash person" and the like, and thus the application is untenable. He answers: "Because it denotes an object in the form of water and so forth.
The meaning is this: since the word *Gaṅgā* and others, being dependent upon the recollection of convention (*saṃketa*), cause one to remember an object that consists precisely of water and so forth.

Therefore, since it is logically impossible for the expressed form— the object such as water— to be construed with the object such as sound, its employment here in its capacity as a signifier (vācaka) is not tenable;
rather, there is the implication (ākṣepa), that is, the drawing forth and introduction, of its own inherent meaning, such as "consisting of water."
Regarding the connection, which is the positive concomitance (*anvaya*):
for that [word] causes one to understand the meaning of the word *taṭa*, it is thus a "connection.
In the view of Bhaṭṭa, denotation (*abhidhā*) is innate (*svābhāvikī*).
The power or function of a word other than that [denotative power] is its *vyāpāra* (operation);
for they do not acknowledge a creator God (*īśvara*), as they accept that linguistic convention has proceeded from beginningless usage.
The view that it was brought forth by a creator God belongs to the Naiyāyikas.
Thus, it has been explained in two ways: that one of these two is natural (*svābhāvikī*), while the other is brought about by God (*īśvarānudbhāvitā*).
This was previously stated in the case of the example, "Kaliṅga is a reckless man."

In subsequent examples such as "the hamlet on the Gaṅgā," because the bank is conveyed by the word "Gaṅgā" in expressions like "the bank of the Gaṅgā," there arises a cognition of identity with the Gaṅgā; thus, the meaning is that the result of *lakṣaṇā* (indication) is the cognition of qualities such as coolness and purity— which reside in the actual object of the Gaṅgā and which are intensified when residing in the object of the bank.
However, some cite "skilled in action" (*karmaṇi kuśalaḥ*) as an example of conventional usage (*rūḍhi*).
Their intention is this:

the primary meaning, which is obtained through etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) as "one who grasps *kuśa* grass" (*kuśagrāhin*), being impossible in the present context, conveys the sense of "dexterous" (*dakṣa*) by means of a connection based on common characteristics such as discernment (*vivekatva*).
Others do not agree with this;

for although the meaning derived from the etymology [of *kuśala*] as "one who grasps grass" (*kuśagrāhin*) is obtainable through linguistic derivation, the primary meaning is that which pertains to "skillfulness" (*dakṣa*).
Indeed, the basis for the etymological derivation of words is one thing, while the basis for their actual application (*pravṛttinimitta*) is another.

If that which is obtained through etymological derivation were considered the primary meaning, then even in the case of "the cow lies down" (*gauḥ śete*), there would have to be figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*);
for the word *go*, derived from the root *gam* with the suffix *ḍe* according to the rule "from *gam*, [the suffix] *ḍe*" (Uṇādi 2.67), is being used at a time when [the animal] is lying down.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, dha) He raises [the following objection] in order to refute the example of conventional indication (*rūḍhilakṣaṇā*) stated by the author of the *Kāvyaprakāśa*: "But some... [He explains:

"Because it is impossible in the present context"—the meaning is that since the word "action" (*karman*) refers here to worldly action, the grasping of *kuśa* grass for the sake of that [action] is impossible.

"Because *dakṣa* alone has the primary meaning"—the sense is that, due to its frequent usage (*bhūriprayoga*) and its lightness (*laghutva*), the unbroken [form] itself is the primary meaning (*mukhyatva*) as the denotable object (*śakyatva*).
"For it is other"—this refers to etymology (*vyutpatti*), which is the sublation of the etymological meaning (*yogārthabādha*).
"Application" (*pravṛtti*) means usage (*prayoga*).
And thus, since the word functions by means of that very cause (nimitta), its primary meaning is precisely that which is delimited by it.
As for the usage [of a word] in a secondary sense (lakṣyārtha), it occurs only when there is a specific intention (tātparya);

for example, the word *kuśala*, which is restricted to one who is dexterous, and the word *maṇḍapa*, which is restricted to a particular type of pavilion, are used in the senses of "one skilled in ritual acts" (*devakarmaṇi kuśala*) and "a sick person" (*rogo maṇḍapa*) respectively, due to their co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with the words *devakarma* and *roga*.
This is because [the word] serves to indicate the intended meaning (*tātparya*).
In the sentence "The cow lies down" (*gauḥ śete*), the phrase "lies down" is used solely for the purpose of indicating that the cow is asleep.
It should be understood that even in the usage "The cow exists" (*gaurasti*) when applied to a sleeping cow, there would be figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
Furthermore, this restriction is not accepted by all;
for since the derivation of *uṇādi* suffixes is only occasional (*prāyika*), they do not occur [in that manner] through such a derivation.

For this very reason, the author of the *Cintāmaṇi* stated: "The *uṇādi* suffixes, which are obtained from the *Pañcapādikā*, [are governed] by the single rule: ‘*uṇādayo bahulam*’ (Uṇādi Sūtra 1.1)."
The intention of Pāṇini, who speaks thus by means of this sūtra, is that the derivation of uṇādi suffixes is merely conventional; and thus there is no linguistic usage based upon such derivation.
Likewise, the word "cow" (go) is employed through its conventional power (ruḍhi-śakti) in a manner common to all cows that go to their own place, specifically in the form of "cowness" (gotva).
It is not by means of derivation through *uṇādi* suffixes. He states its divisions—
Locanā:

"Some, however" (*kecittu*)—by the phrase "skilled in the matter at hand" (*prakṛte karmaṇi kuśalaḥ*), even though [the primary meaning] is possible in terms of its referent, the logical inconsistency is sublated. By the phrase "because the form of a discerning agent is the primary meaning," the sense is: since there is no sublation of the primary meaning here, how can there be indication (*lakṣaṇā*)? Although the word *go* has "going" (*gamana*) as its etymological cause (*vyutpattinimitta*), nevertheless, the very activity of attaining the state of being a cow (*gotvāpatti*) is the cause for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*). For this very reason, the word *go* is applied to a cow whether it is going or coming.
As he said in the context of the word "jar": "Nor is an action consisting in the attainment of that nature [of the jar] intended.
Regarding the phrase "their differences" (*tadbhedān*):

it refers to the distinctions (*viśeṣa*) between those two types of indication (*lakṣaṇā*) mentioned as twofold—based on conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) and purpose (*prayojana*). The term "difference" (*bheda*) is derived from the etymology: "that by which one is divided" (*bhidyate 'nena*).

When the primary meaning implies another meaning for the sake of establishing its connection within the sentence-meaning, this occurs because it also takes up [that other meaning] for itself; thus, this is "indication by inclusion" (upādāna-lakṣaṇā).
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, na) He states its divisions with the words "of the primary meaning" (*mukhyārthasya*).
When the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) is to be understood, [it is as follows].

The meaning is that there is an implication (ākṣepa), that is, a communication, of the other [meaning], namely the non-primary meaning, for the sake of establishing the connection of the primary meaning with the object of the intended purport (tātparya).

Since the connection and the sentence-meaning are non-different, the phrase "for the sake of establishing the connection of the primary meaning in the sentence-meaning" does not constitute a [redundant] connection.
Here too, the word "yayā" (by which) is to be understood as the ellipsis.
He states the derivation of the term *upādāna-saṃjñā* for this [definition]: "it might even apply to the self (*ātman*). This means even to the self in its primary sense.

If, in this context, being the object of the intended meaning (*tātparya-viṣayatva*) were not made a qualifier of the coreferential element (*anvaya*), then there would be an over-narrowness (*avyāpti*) in cases such as "those with umbrellas are going" or "the spears enter."

In this case, since the connection of the pure denoted meaning—which is not the object of the speaker's intention—is possible, there is no implication (ākṣepa) of those [other meanings] such as "those without umbrellas" or "the birds," for the sake of that cognition. It should be noted that when there is a connection with others by virtue of the speaker's intention, the sublation of the pure primary connection occurs precisely through that intention. Furthermore, that sublation consists solely in the impossibility [of the connection] in its form as delimited by the primary characterizer.
It should be understood, however, that there is no impossibility [of the definition] when considered in terms of the form that delimits the denotatum (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*).
An example of the indicative function based on usage (*upādāna-lakṣaṇā*) in the case of conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) is:
"The white one runs" (*śveto dhāvati*).
Regarding purpose (*prayojana*), as in:
"The spears enter.

For here, since the spears and so forth—being insentient and consisting merely of white color and the like—are unable to connect with the actions of running and entering as agents, [the words] serve to establish this by indicating the horses and so forth that are related to them.
And those who are cast down as man-eaters (*puruṣāda*).
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, pa) Connecting here the fact that [the application of] either conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) or a specific purpose (*prayojana*) is the cause for what has been stated regarding the specific and general characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), he provides an example—stating "in the case of conventional usage, [it is] with respect to the material cause (*upādāna*)."
"White" means possessing the quality of whiteness;
"staffs" means "possessing staffs"—this shows the sublation of the primary meaning in these two cases.
Regarding the phrase "in these two": [it refers to the words "white" and "staffs"].
By the word "white and so forth" (*śvetādibhiḥ*), qualities such as blue and so forth are included; by the phrase "spears and so forth" (*kuntādibhiḥ*), other types of weapons are also encompassed.
The phrase "due to being insentient" (*acetanatayā*) is stated precisely with the intention of providing this specific illustration.

In reality, however, in the case of "The umbrella-bearers are going," even though the umbrella-bearers are sentient beings, the universally applicable sublation of the primary meaning (*mukhyārthabādha*) should be understood as simply the non-attainment of the connection with the umbrella, which is the intended object (*tātparyaviṣaya*).
In the phrase "horses, etc.," the word "etc. includes white cows and so forth;
in "men, etc.," the word "etc. includes others such as spear-bearers.

In the former case, the conventional meaning (rūḍhi) prevails due to the absence of a specific purpose; in the latter case, however, the purpose is the extreme density of the *kunta* trees and so forth.
And here, there is also the inclusion of the primary sense, namely the self (*ātman*).
However, in the case of a definition of a definition (*lakṣaṇalakṣaṇā*), it serves as a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for something else; this is the distinction between the two.
This very [type of indication] is called *ajahatsvārthā* (non-abandoning of its own primary meaning).
*Vijñapriyā*:

(vi, pha) "Due to the absence of a purpose"—this means that because there is no consideration of a purpose on the part of one who possesses conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) and so forth, there is an absence [of such a purpose].

A "purpose" (*prayojana*) is the object of the knowledge that serves as the purpose. In this very manner, it should be understood that qualities such as sanctity (*pāvanatva*) and the like are also objects of the term "purpose."
Regarding the phrase "in the case of the definition of the definition"—the word "to be explained" is to be understood as the ellipsis.
By the particle *eva* (only) in the phrase "of the supreme alone," the primary meaning is excluded.
"Indication" (*upalakṣaṇa*) means "presentation" (*upasthāpana*).
Locanā:

(lo, au) "The primary meaning" (*mukhyārtha*)—the primary denoted object; "other than that" (*itarah*) means that which serves as the means for carrying out the subject matter at hand; its "implication" (*ākṣepa*) is its being drawn forth and brought forward.
For the sake of establishing and maintaining the relationship of positive concomitance (anvaya),
because the self is also included as a material cause;
this is the meaning.

In this case, although an object such as a "white spear" (śvetakunta) has already been conveyed by primary denotation (abhidhā), it is again introduced as being indicated (lakṣaṇīya) as a qualifier for the person (puruṣa) and so forth.

This constitutes its "extreme profundity" (atigahanatva). [The phrase] "the persons equipped with spears enter" is not obtainable through primary denotation; this is what is stated by others—this is the ellipsis to be supplied.

The surrendering of one's own primary meaning for the sake of establishing the connection of another [meaning]—because it serves as a cause for secondary indication (upalakṣaṇa)—is this "indication by indication" (lakṣaṇalakṣaṇā). (VisSd 2.7)
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ba) He states the definition of the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇalakṣaṇa*): "the imparting" (*arpaṇam*).
Here, in the phrase "the imparting," the word "only in another" (*paratraiva*) is to be understood as the ellipsis (*śeṣa*).
The meaning is that [the word] has as its object only its own supreme referent (*paramārtha*); however, it does not have even the primary referent (*mukhyārtha*) as its object.
The distinction is that in the case of *upādāna-lakṣaṇā* (metaphorical indication based on appropriation), the primary referent also serves as an object.
In the phrase "of its own" (*svasya*), the word "of which" (*yasyāḥ*) is to be supplied as the remainder.

Thus, when the meaning of the sentence is to be understood, for the sake of establishing the connection—i.e., for the cognition of the connection—of another [word] whose primary sense is not applicable, the "offering of itself" (*arpaṇam svasya*) by that indication (*lakṣaṇā*) consists in having the other alone as its object;
this is the meaning of "indication of indication" (*lakṣaṇalakṣaṇā*).

Since there is no difference between the sentence-meaning and its connection, the phrase "for the sake of establishing the connection of the subsequent [element] with the sentence-meaning" does not constitute a logical connection.

He states the derivation of such a technical term as "upalakṣaṇa": the meaning is that *upalakṣaṇa* is that which, setting aside the primary meaning, causes the cognition of only the secondary meaning, because it serves as the cause for that [cognition].
Indication based on convention (*rūḍhi*) and indication based on purpose (*prayojana*) are illustrated as follows:
"Kaliṅga is a brave man" and "A hamlet on the Gaṅgā.

For in these two cases, the words *kaliṅga* and *gaṅgā* surrender themselves [to their secondary meanings] so that the connection with the meaning of the sentence may be established for the person and the riverbank respectively.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, bha) Regarding the causes of usage based on conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) and specific purpose (*prayojana*), he provides two examples in their respective order, beginning with "Kaliṅga.
Here, the reading is not "Kaliṅga is a reckless person" (*sāhasika*).
However, the reading is simply "Kaliṅga commits a rash act.
The meaning is that this will be clarified in the context of the example for *sādhyavasānā* (exclusive) indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

In both cases, setting aside the primary meanings—the country named Kaliṅga and the riverbank respectively—and in order to bring about the comprehension of the connection with the two other entities—the person residing in that country and the boat—there is a restriction of the scope solely to the person and the boat.
[This refers] to secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
He demonstrates this [with the words]: "of these two, because of the cause.
The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: for the sake of establishing the connection between the person and the bank when the meaning of the sentence is to be understood.
In the phrase "samarpayata," the word "paramātra" (the mere ultimate) is to be understood as the ellipsis; the meaning is "make it the object.

In the phrase "kaliṅgagaṅgāśabdau," the compound "kaliṅgagaṅgāśabda" refers to the two instances of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) residing therein, as should be understood according to the explanation of the meaning provided.
The same should be explained for what follows as well.
Locanā:
(*lo*, *a*) "offering" refers to one's own [body], such as the Gaṅgā and so forth.
The meaning is that because another factor—such as a riverbank (*taṭa*) and so forth—is the cause for the definition (*lakṣaṇa*), it is merely a relation (*sambandha*).
Or, for example:
"Much harm was done there; what more can be said? Yet, supreme goodness has been displayed by you."
"O friend, always acting in this very manner, remain happy for a hundred autumns."
In this case, for the sake of establishing the connection of "doing harm" and so forth with the sentence-meaning, words such as "benefactor" (*upakṛta*) surrender their own literal senses.

Since there is a presentation of "benefit" and so forth toward one who has done harm, there is a subversion of the primary meaning characterized by contrariety; the relationship [between the literal and indicated meanings] is that of contrariety, and the result is the intensification of the harm.
This very [type of compound] is called *jahatsvārtha* ("abandoning its own meaning").
*Vijñapriyā*:
Regarding the state of being caused by a purpose, he states another example: "or as in 'upakṛtam' (a favor done)."
*Pratīyamukti* is a statement made when one's harmfulness has been known from another source;
the meaning is: "Much has been done for you [as a favor]—what can be said in that regard?
However, if the reading is *yatra*, then *tatra* must be supplied.
Regarding the phrase "of harm and so forth"—here, by the word "and so forth" (ādi), wickedness and suffering are included.
"The excellence of harm and so forth as the fruit" means that it is the object of the knowledge that has come to fruition. This should be understood in the same way for each subsequent stage as well.
And this which has been stated is not pleasing.

For if the excellence of the indicated meaning (*lakṣyārtha*) were the purpose, then since that would be possible even in the case of conventional indication (*rūḍhilakṣaṇā*), it would result in there being no distinction [between the types of indication].

Rather, the results of the indications of "doing harm" and "being wicked" are crookedness (*kauṭilya*) on the part of the person addressed, whereas the result of the indication of "being miserable" is crookedness itself.
Locanā:

By the phrase "of those who have done harm" (*apakārārdānām*) and so forth, [the text] refers to wickedness and suffering; by the phrase "this one has been helped" (*upakṛto ’yam*) and so forth, it refers to goodness and happiness.
The excellence of such harm and so forth is not obtainable through the direct denotation of the words themselves.
Each of those [two] is also twofold by way of superimposition (*āropa*) and determination (*adhyavasāna*).
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, ya) It is said to be fourfold because it consists of the two characteristics of grasping (*upādāna*) and definition (*lakṣaṇa*), which are caused by the two factors of conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) and purpose (*prayojana*).
Now, by doubling those four, he describes the eightfold [classification] with the words "superimposition" (āropa) and so forth.

Superimposition (āropa) is the initial superimposition of the denoted meaning (śakyārtha) onto the indicated meaning (lakṣyārtha). The intensification of that superimposition is determination (adhyavasāna).
Those previously mentioned, characterized by fourfold divisions, bring about the cognition of identity with another while the object remains unswallowed. (VisSaD 2.8)

Superimposition (sāropā) occurs when the object [of comparison] is swallowed by the subject [of comparison], while that which is considered "determined" (sādhyavasānikā) occurs when the object is not swallowed by the subject. Superimposition is that which brings about the cognition of identity between the object and the subject itself;
this very [superimposition] is the seed of the figure of speech known as metaphor (rūpaka).
Vijñapriyā:
Regarding the question of what those two become, he says: "of the object" (*viṣayasya*).
The "object" (*viṣaya*) is the locus of superimposition; it is the indicated meaning (*lakṣyārtha*).

The meaning is as follows: for that which is "not swallowed" (*anigīrṇa*)—that is, not covered, meaning expressed by its own denotative word—the identity with another (*anyatādātmya*), which is the non-difference from the primary meaning (*śakyārtha*), constitutes the definition of *sāropā* (superimposition). On the other hand, for that which is "swallowed" (*nigīrṇa*)—specifically, not expressed by its own denotative word—it is considered *sādhyavasānikā* (identification).
Furthermore, the cognition of identity with another must be understood as occurring prior to the knowledge of the secondary signification (lakṣaṇā);
and although it is precisely two words in the same case-ending that effect that cognition, it is not the secondary signification itself.
Nevertheless, the meaning of the phrase "that which produces the cognition of identity with another" is simply that it produces a cognition preceded by the cognition of identity with another.

Nor should it be argued: "In the case of *sādhyavasānā* (metaphorical identification), since there is no word ending in the same case-ending in the absence of a mention by means of a word denoting its own [actual] name, how can it produce a cognition of identity?"
Because when the indicated meaning is expressed by a verb, that [suggested meaning] is perceived;
and this will be demonstrated later.
— *Locanā*:
Thus, each of the four kinds of *lakṣaṇā* is both *sāropā* (superimpositional) and *sādhyavasānā* (identificatory), making eight types in total; thus he says: "Superimposition," etc.

*Āropa* (superimposition) is the cognition of identity with the universal form of the [primary] nature when that nature is not swallowed up (*anigīrṇa*). When the object (*viṣaya*) is swallowed up, the apprehension of non-difference from the subject (*viṣayin*) is *adhyavasāna* (identification).

Thus, although the meaning has already been conveyed by the word's own literal sense, he indicates it through a definition for the sake of clarification: "of the object" (*viṣayasya*). Regarding conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), there is the *sāropā* type of metaphorical indication (*upādāna-lakṣaṇā*), as in:
"The white horse runs."
For here, the horse possessing the quality of whiteness is perceived without its own form being swallowed up, through its identity with the quality inherent in it.
As for the purpose [of such usage], it is as in:
“These spears are entering.”
In this case, because the person wielding the spear is indicated by a pronoun (*sarvanāman*).
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, la):

In the example "The horse is white," the horse possessing the quality of whiteness is the indicated meaning (*lakṣyārtha*), and it is not swallowed up [by the literal sense], because it is expressed by the word "horse" itself.
The cognition of identity between the quality "white" and the horse arises through their sharing the same grammatical case-ending.
Regarding the purpose (prayojana), the phrase "as in the case of 'these are spears'" is used, with the remainder being "characterized as a material cause" (upādānalakṣaṇā).
"These are spears"; [here, the spears are designated by the term for the men carrying them].
In this case, the density of the spears is the purpose [of the expression].
"One possessing spears" (*kuntavān*) is the indicated meaning (*lakṣyārtha*). Because it is expressed by this word, it is not suppressed (*anigīrṇa*).

Regarding the phrase "by means of a pronoun" (*sarvanāmnā*) here: in the *Kāvyaprakāśa*, however, it is stated that when the indicated meaning (*lakṣyārtha*) is denoted by a pronoun, this [metaphor] is exclusively one of superimposition (*sādhyavasāna*), because the word itself—the specific term such as "kunta" (spear)—which expresses its own primary meaning, is not employed.
