This is because it is only when there is a specific mention by a word expressing its own primary meaning that the metaphor is one of identification (*sāropa*).
— *Locanā*:
The horse is the object of superimposition (*āropaviṣaya*).

By the phrase "inhering in itself" (*svasamaveta*), there is a swallowing up (*nigaraṇa*) of the relation—which is the cause for the indication (*lakṣaṇāhetu*)—that consists in inherence (*samavāya*); thus, the white quality is that which is being superimposed.
Immediately after the word "purpose" (*prayojana*), the previously mentioned "indication based on inclusion" (*upādānalakṣaṇā*) characterized as "with superimposition" (*sāropā*) is to be supplied.
The same applies to the subsequent examples. When this [metaphor] occurs through conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), it is a *sāropā* based on a definition (*lakṣaṇalakṣaṇā*). For example:

"In the expression ‘kaliṅgaḥ puruṣo yudhyate’ (a Kalinga man fights), the relation between the Kalinga and the man is that of locus and located (*ādhārādheyabhāva*). As for the purpose (*prayojana*):"
“Clarified butter is longevity” (*āyurghṛtam*).
Here, although clarified butter is the cause of longevity, it is perceived as being identical with longevity through its connection as a related term within the relationship of cause and effect.
Its purpose is the quality of producing longevity, distinguished from other things and characterized by non-deviation.
Or, for example:
when a king’s servant is walking, one says, "The king is walking.
Here, the relationship is characterized by that between master and servant.
Or, for example: "This is a hand" with respect to the portion consisting of its parts, namely the fingertips;
here, the relationship is characterized by the relation between part and whole.
"A carpenter is also a brahmin"— here, [the designation] is characterized by the performance of that function. Regarding pillars intended for Indra, one says, "these are Indras."
In this case, the relationship is characterized by being for that purpose (*tādarthya*);
so it is elsewhere as well.
*Vijñapriyā*:
In the example "The Kalinga is a man," there is no suppression [of the primary meaning] because the indicated sense (*lakṣyārtha*) is expressed by the word "man.
Here, the indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is based on the quality of being a Kalinga.
Regarding the phrase "as in the case of purpose" (*prayojane yathā*), the remainder of the sentence is "in the case of indication based on indication" (*lakṣaṇalakṣaṇā*).
"By way of non-deviation from the distinctness of others"—
thus, both non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) and distinctness from others (*anyavailakṣaṇya*) are stated as the logical reason (*hetu*).
However, in the *Kāvyaprakāśa*, in the example "Clarified butter is life," this distinctness from others constitutes the superimposition (*sāropā*).
In the phrase "this is life" (*āyur idam*), the term is used with a final determinative sense (*sādhyavasānā*); thus, two distinct purposes for these two types [of indication] have been stated.

Having explained *sāropā* indication through the relationship of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), he now demonstrates it by means of other relationships as well—beginning with the example "the king’s body" (*rājārkāya*).
Here, since the word "this" (*asau*) points to the person who is the indicated object (*lakṣyārtha*), there is *sāropā* because of the superimposition (*āropa*) of identity upon the king.

Thus, in both cases, when the referent of the pronoun (*sarvanāman*) indicates the indicated meaning (*lakṣyārtha*), its status as such (*tathātva*) is to be understood. The pillars (*sthūṇāḥ*) are columns in the form of Indra’s banner; the characteristic of being for that purpose (*tādarthyalakṣaṇa*) means having the purpose of his worship.
Here, the motive (*prayojana*) is the state of being worthy of worship like Indra.
*Adhyavasāna* (superimposition) consists in the cognition of the swallowed object as being identical with something else.
Its four varieties have already been illustrated by the previous examples.
Thus, *lakṣaṇā* (indication) is of eight kinds.
Vijñapriyā:

Having thus explained *sāropā*, she now explains the latter part of the verse— "the *sādhyavasānikā* is held [to occur] when [the object] is swallowed"— with the words "furthermore, of that which is swallowed" (*nigīrṇṇasya punar iti*).

Regarding this [indication], there are four varieties of *sādhyavasāna* (indication with superimposition): two types of *upādāna-lakṣaṇā* (indicative indication based on inclusion) in the two cases of conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) and purpose (*prayojana*), and two types of *lakṣaṇa-lakṣaṇā* (indicative indication based on exclusion) in those same two cases.
These are illustrated by the very examples given previously: for *upādāna-lakṣaṇā* in the case of conventional usage, "The white one runs" (*śveto dhāvati*);
and for *upādāna-lakṣaṇā* in the case of purpose, "The spearmen enter" (*kuntāḥ praviśanti*).

Thus, regarding the two examples cited for indication based on conventional usage (*rūḍhi-lakṣaṇalakṣaṇā*), namely "The Kaliṅga commits a rash act," and for indication based on purpose (*prayojana-lakṣaṇalakṣaṇā*), namely "As that royal personage walks, one says 'The king walks,'" the latter is an example where the primary word is abandoned. Therefore, the meaning is that these four are examples of indication where the literal sense is subordinated (*sādhyavasānā*).
In the expression "the king goes" (*rājā gacchati*), the purpose [of the ellipsis] is that he is surrounded by attendants, just like a king.

For in these four cases, since the agent—the object to be characterized—is presented by the verb itself (*ākhyāta*) as the agent, and is not presented by the nominal word (*nāmapada*), there is "swallowing" (*nigīrṇatā*).
And in that case, because the capacity for the primary meaning is superimposed [upon the secondary], it should be understood as being "predominant" (*sādhyavasāna*).

This is because, when a grammatical factor (*kāraka*) is expressed by a word ending in the nominative case, there arises a relation of non-difference (*abhedānvaya*) with the referent of that nominative word.

As for the example of "the hamlet on the Gaṅgā" (*gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*) which is shown as an illustration of indication based on a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇalakṣaṇā*), it is not an illustration of indication where the secondary sense completely absorbs the primary sense (*sādhyavasāna*).
This is because, in that case, the bank—the indicated meaning—is not superimposed with identity upon the flowing current—the primary meaning.

And thus, regarding the definition and example of *lakṣaṇalakṣaṇā* (indirect indication based on indication) that was stated as "Kaliṅga" and so forth, the reading "sāhasikaḥ" (the perpetrator of violence) there is an error.

This is because the person who is the indicated meaning (*lakṣyārtha*) is already expressed by the word "sāhasika" itself; since this constitutes *sāropā* (superimposition), it cannot be *sādhyavasānā* (metaphorical identification).
Rather, the correct reading there should be "kaliṅgaḥ sāhasaṃ karoti" (the Kaliṅga commits violence).

Thus, because the two types of *upādāna-lakṣaṇā* and *alakṣaṇa-lakṣaṇā* are each twofold—being based on either convention (*rūḍhi*) or purpose (*prayojana*)—and because these four are further doubled by their forms as *sāropā* and *sādhyavasānikā*, there are eight varieties.
*Locanā*:
(Lo, u) Having thus shown the fourfold set of examples for *āropa* based on convention and purpose, [the author] now proceeds for the sake of pervading the entire domain [of *lakṣaṇā*].
He states examples according to the difference in relationship, beginning with "yathā vā" (or for example): in the phrase "rājāsau" (that king), as before, the word *adaḥ* (that) reveals the object.
In the phrase "agre," the word *hasta* (hand) is used here even though it refers to the tip (*agra*) of the hand, which is a part of the hand.

Just as one says "the village is burnt" even when only a single part has been consumed by fire, here the word *idam* (this) functions like the word *adas* (that) in the expression "that king over there. He explains the definition of *sādhyavasānā* (metaphorical identification): "of that which is swallowed"—referring to the previous examples such as "the white thing runs."
"The spears enter," "Kaliṅga is a brave man," and "the hamlet on the Gaṅgā"—
all these are pure [metaphors], based on relationships other than similarity. (VisSd 2.9)
"But because of similarity, the secondary [metaphorical] function is considered; by that, it is divided into sixteen types.
Vijñapriyā comments: "He states the sixteen divisions with the words 'by similarity and so forth' (*sādṛśyetara*)."

The other relations, such as the cause-and-effect relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) and so forth, which were previously shown to be of eight kinds, are all "pure" (*śuddha*), meaning they are designated as pure. However, those same eight kinds [of relations] become "secondary" (*gauṇī*) by virtue of the relation of similarity (*sādṛśya*); that is to say, they are designated as secondary because they consist in the connection with the qualities (*guṇa*) residing in the denotable object (*śakyaguṇa*) which constitute the basis for similarity.
Thus, they are divided into sixteen types due to the doubling of the eightfold classification.
Locanā:

(Lo Ū) Thus, it is shown that although there are eight kinds of indication (*lakṣaṇā*), each being either pure (*śuddhā*) or figurative (*gauṇī*), there are sixteen varieties in total—this is indicated by the words "based on similarity or its opposite" (*sādṛśyetara*). The meaning of indication is clear in the commentary (*vṛtti*).
Those previously mentioned eightfold types are *lakṣaṇā* (indication).
Their relations—other than similarity—are those such as cause-and-effect and so forth.
Here, the examples for the pure types are the same as those cited previously.
Vijñapriyā: (vi,
sa) "The very examples mentioned previously"— namely, those beginning with "A white [dog] runs" and ending with "The pillar is for Indra's sake"— all of them indeed.
Because among those [types of secondary indication], there is an absence of even a single instance of a relationship based on similarity (*sādṛśya*).
In the case of conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), that [secondary indication] is based on the literal sense (*upādāna-lakṣaṇā*); it is a figurative (*gauṇī*) one, as in:
"These oils are pleasant in winter."
In this context, the word *taila* (oil) applies to oils such as mustard oil (*sārṣapa*) and others precisely by taking its primary meaning as the oily substance derived from sesame seeds.
Locanā:

(lo, ṛ) Regarding the phrase "these [oils]": since the word *taila* here denotes merely any oil produced from sesame, its primary meaning is set aside (*mukhyārthabādha*) because, in the present context, it is intended to signify something consisting solely of bliss (*sukhamayatva*).

Because there is no [other] purpose, the conventional usage (*rūḍhi*)—which consists in the definition of "appropriation" (*upādāna*)—is recalled by the function [of indication] as being based precisely upon the primary meaning. By the phrase "it exists in oils," since both possess the nature of oiliness (*sneha*), there is a relationship characterized by similarity. By the word "these," through the mention of all [the substances], the nature of *sāropā* (superimposition) is established.
The same should be understood regarding subsequent examples as well.
For instance, with respect to the purpose (*prayojana*):
when princes and those similar to them are walking, one says, "These princes are walking."
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ha) "The primary meaning is the form of the oil-essence of sesame.
Its status as the primary meaning is due to its etymological sense (*yogārtha*) as "that which belongs to sesame" (*tilasyedaṃ*).

Because its function is to produce stickiness (*cikkaṇatā*), here the referent of the word *taila* (oil) consists of both the primary and the indicated meanings, as they share a common basis for similarity; therefore, this is an instance of primary inclusion (*mukhyopādāna*).
In the example "These are princes," the purpose (*prayojana*) is the possession of a beauty equal to that of a prince—the similarity (*sādṛśya*) consisting in having an equal age.

In both cases, because the indicated meaning (*lakṣyārtha*) is grasped by means of the pronoun "these" (*ete*), and because there is a superimposition (*āropa*) of identity with the primary meaning (*śakyārtha*), this is *sāropā* indication.
When it is based on convention (*rūḍhi*), it is an indication by inclusion (*upādāna-lakṣaṇā*) that is metaphorical (*gauṇī*) and characterized by subordination (*sādhyavasānā*), as in:
"Oils are pleasant in winter."
As for [the case of] purpose (*prayojana*), it is as in:
"The princes are going" (*rājakumārā gacchanti*).
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, kṣa) Regarding the type of metaphorical identification (*sādhyavasānā*) based on similarity, he says "oil" (*tailāni*).
Here, because the denoted meaning is not presented by means of a pronoun (*sarvanāma*), it is not *sāropā* (metaphorical identification with superimposition);

rather, since the denoted meaning is presented by the word "pleasure" (*sukha*), which—while not excluding the primary meaning—is common to both the primary and the indicated meanings, there is a state of being swallowed (*nigīrṇatā*) consisting in the concealment of that [primary] meaning.
Therefore, because of the superimposition of identity with the meaning of the possible [referent], it is *sādhyavasānā* (predicative). In the example "the prince" (*rājakumāra*),
since the agents who are the indicated meanings are presented by the verbal suffix itself, they are swallowed up (*nigīrṇṇatā*).
In this case, there is a superimposition of identity upon the prince Śakya; thus, it is a *sādhyavasānā* (metaphor with complete absorption).
The purpose is the possession of equal beauty, and the similarity consists in being of equal age.
In the case of conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), that [indication] is called *lakṣaṇalakṣaṇā*; it is secondary (*gauṇī*) as follows:
"The king cleanses the thorn of the Lord of Gauḍa.
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, ka) Regarding the phrase "the King [conquered] the Lord of Gauḍa":
here, the Lord of Gauḍa—who, by virtue of causing pain, is similar to a thorn—is the indicated meaning (*lakṣyārtha*), and it is expressed by its own word (*svaśabda*).
Here, because there is a superimposition (*āropa*) of identity with the thorn, it is *sāropā* (superimpositional).
Regarding purpose (*prayojana*):

as in "The Vāhīka is an ox. Regarding conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), there is the secondary indication (*gauṇī*) characterized by indication (*lakṣaṇalakṣaṇā*) with complete identification (*sādhyavasānā*);
as in "The king cleanses the thorns."
As for [the usage] based on purpose (*prayojana*), for example: "The cow speaks" (*gaur jalpati*). *Vijñapriyā* explains: "The Vāhīka is a cow" (*gaur vāhīkaḥ*).
The Vāhīka is a plow-drawer,
and he is already included by his own name;
there is a similarity based on the quality of ignorance.
Stupidity, dullness, and so forth, or lack of cleverness, constitute the purpose;
the reading "the king is a thorn," written as a series of meanings, is merely a scribal error,
because the intended meaning is not conveyed by any word therein.
Firstly, because the superimposition of identity with the possible [meaning] is untenable there;
rather, the reading is simply "the thorn is removed by the king."

In that case, when the object to be purified (*śodhya*) is presented by the verb as the object of the action (*karman*), the superimposition (*āropa*) of identity (*tādātmya*) upon the denoted meaning of the subject word ending in the nominative case occurs.

Even in the expression "the cow speaks" (*gaur jalpati*), since it is impossible for a cow to be a speaker, the superimposition of identity with the cow occurs upon the speaker who is presented by the verb and whose own nature is swallowed up (*nigīrṇa*); this is therefore a case of *sādhyavasāna* (predicative) metaphor.
The purpose [of this] is cleverness (*vaidagdhyam*), just as in the case of [the metaphor] "like a cow."
The similarity [is established] by way of insentience and so forth.
Locanā:

(lo, ṝ) Following the word "purpose" (*prayojana*), the phrase "metaphorical indication based on material cause" (*upādānalakṣaṇā*), "superimposition" (*sāropā*), and "secondary" (*gauṇī*) are to be supplied.
The same mode of operation as previously stated applies to the subsequent examples as well.
Regarding the word "these" (*ete*):
here, because the term "prince" (*rājakumāra*) is applied to those who resemble princes, there is a sublation of the primary meaning (*mukhyārthabādha*).
Similarity is the relationship [between objects] through such means as valor, beauty, and attire;
the purpose of these is excellence.

Regarding the word *lāja*—in the case of its use by the Lord of Gauḍa (the poet Govardhana) with the word *kaṇṭaka*, it is based on conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) because there is no specific purpose for employing that term.
The relationship [between the word and its referent] is similarity, consisting in the infliction of trivial suffering.
Because the primary meaning of the word "thorn" (*kaṇṭaka*) is abandoned in this context, it is *lakṣaṇalakṣaṇā* (indication by means of a characteristic).
Since the domain of the King of Gauḍa is not swallowed up [into the word], it is of the nature of *sāropā* (superimposition).

In this example, "The Vāhīka is an ox" (*gaur vāhīkaḥ*), just as there is a secondary (*gauṇī*) indication based on a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇalakṣaṇā*) with superimposition (*sāropā*) for a specific purpose,
so too will it become clear later in the commentary itself.
Likewise, in the case of "The ox speaks" (*gaur jalpati*), there is also a secondary indication based on a defining characteristic with identification (*sādhyavasānā*) for a specific purpose.

On this point, some say: "The qualities such as dullness and sluggishness, which coexist with the cow, are indicated; and these serve as the grounds for the word 'cow' denoting the Vāhīka. This is incorrect.

Because it is impossible for the word "cow" to denote the meaning of a Vāhīka person when the conventional relationship [between the word and that object] has not been grasped, and because it merely conveys the meaning of the word "cow" alone; furthermore, since the primary denotative function (*abhidhā*) has ceased, and that which has ceased does not arise again.
*Vijñapriyā*:
Regarding the phrase "here some [say]": the meaning is that the own-meaning (*svārtha*) is "cowness" (*gotva*), which refers to those things that coexist with it.
Regarding the phrase "in the denotation of the Vāhīka object": the meaning is "in its presentation by means of the primary function" (*abhidhā*).
Regarding the phrase "they become the cause": the meaning is "they become the delimiters of the capacity for denotation" (*śakyatāvacchedaka*).
And thus, according to their established doctrine, the Vāhīka is [cognized] by the power of the form "insentience" itself, such that there is the cognition "the Vāhīka is insentient.
This is incorrect.

And this fault arises precisely because of their failure to accept that [conventional] doctrine; for they have established as their settled tenet that the capacity to convey the denotatum is grasped through indication (lakṣaṇā) with respect to the substratum (dharmin) itself.

The phrase "the meaning of the word 'cow'" implies that once a word has been uttered, its function of conveying the meaning ceases according to the nature of words, and thus the primary denotation (abhidhā) also comes to an end.
— *Locanā*

Now, demonstrating that the secondary function (*gauṇī vṛtti*) is included within indication (*lakṣaṇā*) by means of refuting the prima facie objection (*pūrvapakṣa*), [the author] says "here," intending to show that all will be consistent by removing any disagreement even regarding a single example.
In the case of "The *vāhīka* is a cow" (*gaur vāhīkaḥ*), the word "cow" has its own primary meaning (*svārtha*).

Those qualities are "indicated" (*lakṣita*) there because they are indicated and understood through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*); by the use of the particle *ca*, it is implied that their status as mere objects of indication does not suffice for rest [in the meaning], but rather they serve as the cause (*nimitta*) for the denotation and the cognition of the referent "Vāhīka" through primary denotation (*abhidhā*).

The intention is that because there is no further arising [of the primary meaning], there is an absence of operation once [the denotation] has ceased— according to the maxim regarding sound, cognition, and action— and furthermore, to postulate another denotative function (abhidhā) would involve the fault of conceptual complexity (kalpanā-gaurava).
Moreover, others hold that the meaning of a *vāhīka* is not denoted by the word "cow" (*go*).

However, it is argued that by virtue of the similarity between the qualities associated with the primary meaning and those residing in the *vāhīka*, it is precisely those qualities [of the *vāhīka*] that are indicated (*lakṣyante*).
Others, however, do not accept even this.
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, gha) "Only the qualities are perceived"—the meaning is that the cognition of the Vāhīka [person] arises through implication (*ākṣepa*).
Locanā:
(lo, e) He states another opinion with the words "others."
It is not so designated because of the very principle already stated:
the word "cow" has its own primary meaning;
however, through the relation of generic similarity, qualities such as dullness and sluggishness residing in the Vāhīka person [are intended].
By the particle *eva* (only) here, there is an exclusion of the possessor of qualities (*guṇin*).
They are "indicated," meaning they are understood through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*); this refers even to that other view mentioned immediately prior. For instance:
In this case, is the meaning "Vāhīka" understood from the word *go* itself, or not?
If it is, is it understood from the word *go* alone,
or from a quality indicated [by it]?
Or is it because of invariable concomitance?
In that regard, it is not the first [option],
because this [word] has not been conventionally assigned to the object "Vāhīka."
Locanā:

(lo, ai) In this context, "in the first case" refers to the position of direct cognition (*pratītipakṣa*). "From the indicated quality" means from qualities residing in itself, such as dullness, sluggishness, and so forth.
Inseparable relation (*avinābhāva*) is a non-deviating connection; through that [connection], by its power, there occurs the state of being implied and so forth.
The first case is the position that a Vāhīka is understood from the word "cow" alone. And this understanding is brought about by denotation (*abhidhā*).
Not the second [alternative],
because an object obtained through inseparable connection (avinābhāva) cannot enter into a verbal syntactic relation;
for a verbal expectancy is fulfilled by a word alone.
Not the second [alternative];
for if the meaning "Vāhīka" were not understood from the word "go," then the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between this [word] and the word "vāhīka" would be inconsistent.
Vijñapriyā:
"Even in the first case" means in the position that the word "cow" (*gośabda*) brings about the cognition of a *vāhīka* [barbarian].
The refutation of that is expressed by the phrase "not the first."

Regarding the phrase "because it is not conventional" (asaṃketitatvāt)— it should be noted that the refutation of this very point has already been demonstrated according to that [opponent's] own view.

Nor is the second position tenable— the view that there is a cognition [of the object] through implication (ākṣepa) based on the inseparable connection (avinābhāva) with the qualities indicated by the word.
"Because it is impossible for [the meaning] to enter into verbal comprehension"—this has been stated solely with the intention of one's own established doctrine (*svasiddhānta*).

In reality, however, just as in the theory that the word's power resides in the universal (*jātiśaktivāda*), where the individual (*vyakti*)—which is obtained through the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) with the universal—enters into verbal comprehension, there is no sublation here either if the same were the case.
"Not the third"—referring to the position that there is no cognition of a *vāhīka* from the word "cow."
"Co-referentiality" (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) means the state of having the same case-ending, which is necessarily characterized by conveying the non-difference between their respective referents.
*Locanā*:
(lo, o) The meaning is that [this relation] is obtained through inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*), but not conveyed by words.

The teacher states his agreement with the words beginning with "śābdī" (verbal), etc.: for [the meaning] is conveyed by the word itself, and not by a meaning obtained through invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) and so forth.
The third alternative is not perceived as a position.

Therefore, in this case, the word "cow" (*go*), failing to obtain syntactic connection (*anvaya*) with the word "Vāhīka" through its primary function (*mukhyavṛtti*), indicates the object "Vāhīka" due to a relationship based on common properties such as ignorance (*ajñatva*).
The purpose is to convey the excellence [of the speaker] through the ignorance of the Vāhīka.
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, ca):
For instance, the meaning of the word "cow" (*go*) is the quality of dullness, sluggishness, and so forth, residing in the Vāhīka.
The word *vāhīka* has as its primary meaning a horse-drover (*halavāhika*).
It indicates the meaning of *vāhīka*—namely, by way of its similarity to a cow; this is the implied sense. —Locanā.
(Lo, Au) In response to the inquiry as to what the destination (*gati*) of that [word] might be, he states his own view with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).
The meaning is: because there is no other destination in this manner.
The word "cow" (*go-śabda*) is the referent of the word "cow."
This is due to the metaphorical treatment of the word and its meaning as non-different.
In other such instances as well, it should be understood in this same way.
The primary function [of a word] is denotation (*abhidhā*).
The meaning "the Vāhīka is ignorant" is not obtainable through the primary denotation of its own words;

since this function called *gauṇī* (metaphorical) is caused by the triad of factors beginning with the sublation of the primary meaning (*mukhyārthabādha*), its inclusion within *lakṣaṇā* (indication) is indeed clear—this is the intended sense.
And here, through the cognition of identity between the Gaṅgā and the bank, there is an excellence of coolness and so forth in the bank.

The claim by Paṇḍita Caṇḍīdāsa that— in the expression "the Vāhīka is a cow"— the excessive dullness and so forth in the Vāhīka is perceived through the cognition of identity (*tādātmya*) between the words "cow" and "Vāhīka," and therefore this metaphorical effort (*upacāra*) of the author of the *Kāvyaprakāśa* is useless, is an unexamined statement.

For indeed, the function [of a word] does not occur with indifference toward the relationship in cases other than those involving similarity, as it does in the case of two things related by similarity.
For this very reason, others have stated that there is a direct relationship between the indicator (*lakṣaka*) and the indicated (*lakṣya*),
whereas similarity— such as in the case of "the *vāhīka* is an ox"— consists in the commonality of their attributes, and is not of that [direct] nature.

Therefore, while in some cases— such as on a riverbank— there may indeed be some degree of coolness and so forth due to its connection with the Gaṅgā and the like, when it is communicated by the word "Gaṅgā," that coolness and so forth is perceived as something additional upon the cognition of "Gaṅgā-ness.
However, in the case of a Vāhīka, there is never the possibility of qualities residing in a cow being present [in him].
However, [the identification] applies only to those of the same class.
Furthermore, even when it is said, "The Vāhīka is a cow," the cognizer does not in any way apprehend identity;
rather, due to the use of grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), there is merely the suppression of that [apprehension of difference].
This has been stated by Vācaspatimiśra in his *Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣyavyākhyā*: “Furthermore, a word for one thing is applied to another through connection with qualities perceived in that other;
where there is such agreement between the speaker and the listener, that is the secondary (gauṇa) usage, and it is preceded by the cognition of difference.”
And this [metaphor] is called *gauṇī* (secondary) because of its connection with qualities (*guṇa*);
the former, however, is *śuddhā* (pure) because it is unmixed with figurative usage (*upacāra*).

For figurative usage (*upacāra*) indeed consists merely in the concealment of the perception of difference between two words that are utterly distinct, by virtue of the power of an excellence of similarity.
For example,
as in the case of "the two young Brahmins" or "the two white cloths," there is no perception of absolute difference;
therefore, in such instances, the indication (lakṣaṇā) is purely primary (śuddhā).
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, cha) "On account of the connection with qualities" means on account of the connection with qualities such as dullness that belong to the same class as the dullness and other qualities residing in a capable cow.
"The former," however, refers to "a white cloth."
The meaning is that [the example] begins with "Clarified butter is life" (*āyur ghṛtam*) and so forth.

Now, one might object: even there, by virtue of having the same case-ending, there is indeed a metaphorical application (*upacāra*) of identity between "life" and "clarified butter"; to this he replies: "For the metaphor...
By the mention of having the same case-ending, the non-mixture [of the two referents] through metaphor is not the cause of the purity [of the primary sense].
However, the sense is that it occurs only when there is similarity (*sādṛśya*) in that very case.
As for the phrase "of the white cloth," it should also be understood as "of life and ghee."—
Locanā.

(Lo, a) Intending this, he demonstrates the distinction between the figurative (*gauṇa*) and the pure (*śuddha*) types of indication (*lakṣaṇā*) and qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*) in the manner already described by the words "And this" (*iyaṃ ca*).
This [indication] is caused by a relationship of similarity (*sādṛśya*), arising from a connection with qualities (*guṇayoga*), and not from a direct relationship.
By the phrase "called metaphorical transfer (*upacāra*) between two things that are utterly distinct," he indicates the nature of the relationship.
Directness has been demonstrated;
there is merely a concealment, but not an absolute non-existence.
For, according to the method already stated, because the relation is direct, there is no perception of absolute difference.
Indications characterized by a result (phalalakṣaṇā) are of two kinds, according to whether the suggested meaning (vyaṅgya) is concealed or unconcealed. // VisSd_2.10 //

The eight varieties of indication (*lakṣaṇā*) shown in relation to purpose (*prayojana*) each become twofold— according to whether the suggested meaning in the form of the purpose is hidden (*gūḍha*) or manifest (*agūḍha*)— thus resulting in sixteen varieties. Among these, the "hidden" is that which is perceivable only by those whose intellectual capacity has been ripened through the cultivation of the meaning of poetry.
For example:
"Much was done there...
This is the unhidden [suggestion], which is perceivable by all people due to its extreme clarity.
As it is said:
"It is the intoxication of youth alone that teaches graceful charms to amorous women."

In this context, by the term "teaches" (*upadiśati*), "manifests" (*āviṣkaroti*) is indicated; and the excellence of this manifestation is clearly perceived, just like the subject matter itself. *Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, ja) Indications characterized by results (*phalalakṣaṇā*) are those that possess a purpose (*prayojanavatyaḥ*).
Since it has been shown that there are eight varieties in the case of a purpose— eight being established in the conventional sense (*rūḍhau*) and eight in the case of a purpose—
it is said that for those with matured intellects, cognition arises from firm mental impressions (*saṃskāra*).

Regarding the phrase "upakṛtam" (a favor has been done): according to the author's own view, this refers to an excess of injury; however, according to another view, it refers to the motive of the injurer, such as deceitfulness, which is accessible only to those who are experts in discerning the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*).
Because the meaning of "mockery" (*solluṇṭhana*) is not perceivable by those who lack refinement.
Regarding the phrase "he reveals": the sense is that since being an instructor is a quality belonging to a guru, it is sublated by the intoxication of youth.
And regarding the phrase "an excellence of revelation": this, however, has been stated as something beyond ordinary experience.

In the *Kāvyaprakāśa*, however, the imparting of instruction (*śikṣādāna*) alone is the indicated meaning (*lakṣyārtha*). In that context, "effortlessness" (*anāyāsa*) is the purpose (*prayojana*), which, like the expressed meaning, is known by all people. For that purpose is perceived within the imparting of instruction—the indicated meaning—as a property of the sentence-meaning; namely, that through instruction, effortlessness in learning is indeed known by all people. This is the intention [of the author], as stated in the *Locanā*.

(Lo, ā) Now, he demonstrates the different types of indication (*lakṣaṇā*) precisely through the variety of the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*); "of the suggested" means the result or purpose, and indication is that which is joined with such a result.
These are graceful modes of expression.

Based precisely on these two—the suggested meaning being either hidden or unhidden—two specific varieties of poetry will be described, known as *dhvani* (suggestion) and *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya* (subordinated suggestion).
Furthermore, these [modes] are also twofold according to whether the result resides in the substratum (*dharmin*) or in the attribute (*dharma*).

These sixteen varieties of *lakṣaṇā* (indication) mentioned immediately above become thirty-two varieties when each is divided into two types—those residing in the substratum (*dharmigata*) and those residing in the attribute (*dharmagata*). To give a mere illustration:

“The sky is smeared with the glossy, dark luster of clouds; the clouds are heavy with quivering cranes; the winds are laden with spray; and the soft cries of joy from the peacocks, friends of the rain-clouds, resound.”
Granted, let it be; I am Rāma, firm and hard-hearted, and I shall endure everything. But what will become of Vaidehī? Alas, alas! O Queen, be steadfast.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, jha) "Of sixteen kinds" means having the form of hidden and non-hidden purposes. "By way of being included within the subject and the property" [is the meaning].
*Dharma* is the indicated meaning (*lakṣyārtha*).

*Dharma*, however, is the referent (*padārtha*) residing in the indicated meaning, as in the expression "glossy-dark" (*strigdha-śyāmalā*). This is an utterance by Rāma, separated from Sītā when the rainy season has arrived. [The clouds] are such that they possess flickering, restless cranes (*valākā*).
The meaning is: "Let these [clouds], which are the friends of the peacocks—the kindlers of separation—exist as they please; nevertheless, they are not able to kill me.
For I am Rāma;
I am one who endures suffering.
He states the reason for this being so with the word "kaṭhora" (harsh).
Therefore, the meaning is: "I endure all of this, beginning with the heavy rains.
Vaidehī, however, was not like that.
"How will it be? means "of what kind will it be? "Hā hā" expresses distress.
Therefore, O Queen Vaidehī,
be steadfast— meaning, be one who endures suffering.
Here, the excellence of that very quality [of fortitude] is the fruit, with respect to the subject Rāma, who is characterized by the capacity to endure extreme suffering.
In the expression "a hamlet on the Ganges" (*gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*), the result is the excellence of qualities such as coolness and purity [inferred] in the riverbank.
*Vijñapriyā*:

Regarding "Rāma is indicated"—the meaning is that Rāma is indicated by way of his being capable of enduring suffering, because his being Rāma is the cause for the presence of excitants (*uddīpaka*) such as the clouds.
"The excellence of that very [quality]" means that the excellence of Rāma himself—who is capable of enduring suffering—is of the nature of separation (vipralambha);
and here, the excellence of his capacity to endure suffering is indeed perceived.
Therefore, it must be asked: why was this not shown as an example of excellence residing in a quality (dharma)?
Because that too, due to the lack of distinction from the intended object, is simply a property (dharma) residing in the subject (dharmī);

for instance, the inability to endure suffering is merely the absence of aversion toward suffering, and since it is of the nature of an absence, its "excellence" consists precisely in the absence of any further excellence and the absence of aversion in general.
And that [absence] is not a distinct category of entity (padārtha).
But it is indeed of the nature of non-existence,
precisely because it resides in the substratum (dharmin) whose form is Rāma.
Regarding the phrase "of the excellence of coolness and purity"— since there is no further excellence beyond excellence, the meaning is "of that which possesses an excellence of coolness and purity."

In this context, it should be understood that the element of excellence (*atiśayita-aṃśa*) serves no further purpose and arises merely by way of incidental occurrence. One might object: "Why could the coolness and purity residing in the *dharma* (the property) itself not be the purpose here? This is not so; for the coolness and purity of the bank are indeed real (*vāstavika*) due to its connection with the Gaṅgā.

Consequently, since those two qualities can be recalled through the recollection of their relata once the bank is cognized via secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the intended meaning is that the purpose lies precisely in the excellence of those two qualities, which are thus devoid of the restriction of being merely suggested (*vyaṅgyatva-niyama-rahitayoḥ*).
Locanā:
(lo, i) "Snigdha" means moving or undulating;

In the word *giri*, it means speech; in *girīṇām*, it means heavy; and in *guru*, it means excellent.
Furthermore, in *gām*, it means the earth and the bull.
Vibhūti means prosperity as well as ashes;
Umāvallabha, Bhānudeva, and Īśvara [are names of Śiva],
because they are to be described in this particular context.

And here, since the meaning of Maheśvara—which is not the primary subject—perceived by the word *umāvallabha* was previously unrelated [to the context], the relationship of standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and object of comparison (*upameya*) is postulated between Maheśvara and King Bhānu;

thus, the suggestion of a simile (*upamā-dhvani*) in the form "as if he were Umāvallabha" is understood through suggestion (*vyañjanā*) alone. This is the intended sense of the particle *eva* (only/just) in this instance: namely, that in the word *umāvallabha*, the cognition of the second meaning ceases once the denotative function (*abhidhā*) has conveyed only the primary meaning, and because the indicative function (*lakṣaṇā*) is dependent upon the cognition of a primary meaning.

Since *tātparya* (implicatory power) is necessarily restricted to conveying only the connection between what is denoted by primary signification (*śakti*) and what is indicated by secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*), the fourth function called *vyañjanā* (suggestion) must indeed be accepted.
Now, one might object that even here, according to the view that "there is a difference in words due to a difference in meaning," there exists a duality of distinct words;
and this [duality] is the cause for the delusion of identity based on their similarity.

And if it is argued: "Since the primary denotative function (*abhidhā*) ceases after conveying the meaning 'king' through the word *umāvallabha* and so forth at the outset, let a second word convey the second meaning by means of its power of denotation residing therein;
what is the need for postulating another mode of operation (*vṛtti*)?"—this is not correct.
For if two words were postulated here, how could the perception of the contextual meaning be experienced as occurring first?
Because it is impossible for there to be a fixed sequence of priority and posteriority between two things when both are intended as denotable meanings (*abhidheya*).

Likewise, in cases such as "bewilderment, languor," and so forth, even if the word *viṣa* signifies poison (*garala*), its power of denotation (*abhidhā*) is not revived by the proximity of words such as *bhujaṅga*;
rather, the function [of the word] is solely suggestion (*vyañjanā*).

However, in this context, the cause for the comprehension of a second meaning is verbal in cases such as *bhujaṅga* (serpent/lover), while it is contextual (*ārtha*) in cases such as *durgālaṅghitā* (unassailable by Durgā/unassailable by a fortress).

But in cases such as *yena dhvastam*, because there is no restrictive factor, there is doubt regarding multiple meanings; and in cases such as *vyathāṃ dvayeṣām api medinībhṛtām*, the learned Caṇḍīdāsa maintains that both meanings are expressed.

We shall refute this on the occasion of explaining the figure of speech *śleṣa* (punning). Furthermore, regarding the verse beginning with "durgālaṅghitā," the Master Mahima—who asserts the non-existence of the second meaning which is established by direct experience—practically keeps his eyes closed like an elephant; for he rejects the second meaning of the great poets such as Vyāsa and Vālmīki solely through a succession of bad explanations and faulty instructions.
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that such a poetic composition would be fruitless;
furthermore, since both meanings are equally perceived, there would be a lack of authority for concluding with a specific interpretation.

Moreover, rather than postulating a new substratum (dharmin) to convey the second meaning, it is better to postulate a new attribute (dharma); thus, because it involves the postulation of a distinct function, it is appropriate to accept a distinct operation called *vyañjanā* (suggestion).
However, where that [function] extends too far, out of fear of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), it is accepted as denotation (*abhidhā*) by virtue of its being a relation; thus everything is clear.
He states that which is based on indication (*lakṣaṇāmūla*): "That for the sake of which indication is resorted to is the purpose (*prayojana*)."
That by which [an object] is made known would be *vyañjanā* (suggestion), based upon *lakṣaṇā* (indication).
Locanā:
(lo, o) "Rooted in characteristics" means that it has not yet reached the stage of formal instruction; this is the remainder [of the sense]. It is "worshipped," meaning it is honored.
That [function] by which— on account of which, for which purpose, and in whatever manner through the power of the word—

as in the case of "A hamlet on the Gaṅgā" (*gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*) and so forth, after the primary signification (*abhidhā*) has ceased because it has conveyed meanings such as "consisting of water," and after the secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) has ceased because it has conveyed meanings such as "the bank," there is conveyed an excellence such as coolness and purity,
is suggestion (*vyañjanā*) based upon secondary signification (*lakṣaṇāmūlā*).
Having thus explained the verbal indication (*śabdī vyañjanā*), he now states the fourfold [indication] of meaning (*arthī*):
"Of the speaker, the person to be addressed, and the sentence; of another's proximity and of the expressed meaning; of the context, place, time, tone of voice, gestures, and so forth. (ViSd 2.16)
The term "vyañjana" is connected [to the previous].
Vijñapriyā:
"For the sake of whom."
The meaning is: that which is the cause for the cognition [of it].
"Due to distinction" means due to difference. — *Locanā*
(Lo, Au) He states the connection with the context by saying "thus" (*evam*). That which is to be made known is "the object of cognition" (*boddhavya*).
Since the employment of words is for the sake of another, the meaning is: that [subject] in which an apprehension inheres is established as such.
That which is expressed and conveyed by a word is the "denoted" (vācya).
By this, there is the inclusion of the threefold meaning consisting of the denoted (vācya), the indicated (lakṣya), and the suggested (vyaṅgya).
"Context" (prastāva) refers to the specific situation or topic.
*Kākū* is a modification of sound;
it is due to *vaiśiṣṭya*, meaning "distinction" or "peculiarity," which applies respectively to each of the factors such as the speaker and so forth.
*Anyam* means "different from," specifically distinct from the previously mentioned denotative meanings and other such elements.

Regarding the excellence of the speaker, the statement, the context, the place, and the time, as in my own verse: “The season is spring, and this flower-bowed god of love is enraged; the breezes blow steadily, removing the fatigue of passion; even this pleasure-grove is charming with its thickets of *vañjula* trees; yet the husband is far away—tell me, what is to be done today?”
"Let a secret lover be sent quickly by you to this place"—this is indicated by a certain woman to her friend.
*Vijñapriyā* explains:
"At the [proper] time."
By the word "this" (eṣa), the intoxicating nature of desire being experienced at that very moment is indicated.
By the word "husband" (pati)— meaning the supporter and master, and not merely the beloved—
there is here a specific distinction on the part of the speaker due to her being overwhelmed by passion and so forth.
By the sentence’s being endowed with such a perceived charm;
by the context’s [suggesting] the husband’s distant presence and so forth;
and by the location’s being a pleasure grove characterized by *vakula* thickets and the like.

By virtue of the season being like spring; thus, through this figurative expression (*vakrokti*) characterized by their specific qualities, the manifestation of the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgyārtha*) is indeed clear.
(vi, na) "The season is sweet"—this is a statement by a woman whose husband is away, addressed to her female friend.
The meaning is clear. "In this place" refers to this location in the form of a pleasure grove (*kelīvanī*).

For the comprehension of such a suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*), there is the speaker’s sentence, which serves the purpose of inquiry regarding what is to be done by pointing out that [grove]; and there is the season of spring, which has acquired the context of love (*śṛṅgāra*) through the display of excitants (*uddīpana*).
And dissimilarity (*vailakṣaṇya*) is the logical reason (*hetu*).
Locanā:
For example, regarding the excellence of that which is to be understood:

"The sandalwood paste has completely washed away from your breasts; the redness is rubbed off from your lower lip; your eyes are entirely devoid of collyrium; and this slender body of yours is covered in horripilation—O messenger, you liar!"
"Since your kinsmen do not know how you have come to suffer, you went from here to bathe in the pond, and not to that base man."
Vijñapriyā:

"Niḥśeṣa" etc.— this is a sarcastic remark by the heroine directed at a female messenger who, having been sent to bring the lover, has returned after being enjoyed by him, and is thus deceiving her by saying, "Even at my request, he did not come."
O messenger, you who speak falsely, saying that he did not come even at my request;
you went from here to the pond to bathe because your kinsmen were suffering from the onset of an unknown passion, but you did not go to the presence of that base man.
The construction is not "to bathe in the pond," because the verbal root *snā* (to bathe) is intransitive (*akarmaka*).
[The author] first shows the actions resulting from bathing: "without remainder," and so forth.

For this reason, the surface of your breasts and their sides are completely stripped of sandalwood paste; your lower lip has its redness wiped away; and your eyes have become entirely devoid of collyrium, as much as possible. (This is the implied sense.)
And that word "distant" (*dūram*) is an adverbial modifier of the action.
Likewise, this slender and emaciated body of yours is "thrilled" (*pulakitā*); the meaning is that it has become covered with horripilation due to the coldness of the bath.
*Tathā* means "and so," used here as a conjunction to collect the qualifiers.
*Locanā*:
(*lo*, *ā*) *Niḥśeṣa*—*taṭa* means "nearby."
And that region was level;
there, the sandalwood paste had been rubbed away without remainder,
yet a trace remained on the nipples and other parts.
The lower lip has its redness wiped away;
the collyrium is far from the eyes, yet it is smeared near them;
the remnants of the collyrium are indicated here and there.

This body, though it has been bathed for a long time, is now bristling with horripilation; it is slender and emaciated. It belongs to a base man, one who was previously observed to have taken a lowly wife.

In this case, by means of *viparītalakṣaṇā* (indication through the opposite), what is indicated (*lakṣya*) is: "You have gone to that very place to sport. And the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) to be conveyed—namely, "in order to sport"—is understood from the specific character of the female messenger (*dūtī*).
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, pha) "You have gone" is the indicated meaning (*lakṣya*).
Since the falling of sandalwood paste and so forth are perceived precisely as effects of sexual pleasure, they lead to the cognition of departure from that [pleasure];
thus, the opposite of that—namely, actual departure—is the meaning indicated by figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

For these two are understood as having the function of providing pleasure; thus, by the wiping away of the falling [sandalwood paste] from the lower lip and the removal of the collyrium, it would have been stated that there was merely washing during bathing.

Likewise, having reached the corners of the eyes which were touched by kissing at a distance while being uncolored, it would have been stated that the entire eye was devoid of collyrium during bathing.
Likewise, there is no greatness in the death of Candana, for at that time, when the summer season had arrived, he was without horripilation due to bathing;
furthermore, since there was no fault in approaching him, it is improper to call him "low-born," as his status as a low-born person is already established by his very nature as a procuress.
Regarding the statement that "going" here is [conveyed] through indication (*lakṣaṇā*), this is disapproved by the author of the *Kāvyaprakāśa*.
According to his view, it is precisely the act of going to her presence for the sake of dalliance that is the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*).
For, since the sentence "you have not gone" possesses the status of poetry (*kāvyatva*), there is no indication at all in that context.
Thus it has been said: "There is no primary denotative power (śakti) nor even indication (lakṣaṇā) in a sentence.
However, indication in a word is simply not possible here, because the act of going is already expressed by the verbal root *gam*.
As for the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*), its purpose is fulfilled precisely through its connection with the act of going to the well.
Even if metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is admitted in the case of a sentence, it is still not [the primary function here],
because according to that school's view, the act of going to her presence for the purpose of dalliance is what is first suggested (*vyaṅgya*).
For instance, since the falling of sandalwood paste and so forth are initially perceived as being caused by bathing, no contradiction arises [that would necessitate a figurative sense].
Because the qualification regarding the reconnection [of meaning] occurs only at a later time, since the sublation (bādhā) has already entered;
and in this case, it is the operation of *vyañjanā* (suggestion), not of *lakṣaṇā* (indication),
because the operation of *lakṣaṇā* occurs precisely when the sublation first enters.
As it has been said:
"In some cases there is the appearance of something as being sublated; in other cases, there is the sublation of what has appeared.
In the former case, there would be only indication (lakṣaṇā); in the latter, however, there is only denotation (abhidhā)."
Thus:

in the preceding case, since it was first presented as being cognized through sublation (bādhyatayā), by the phrase "but [it is] indeed denotation" (abhidhaiva tu), it was indicated that there is no indication (lakṣaṇā) therein;
subsequently, it was stated that going to his presence in order to sport is expressed solely through suggestion (vyañjanā).
In this context, the presence of sandalwood paste, cyuta, and so forth, should be understood as the distinguishing characteristic of the messenger (*dūtī*) who is to be recognized.
Locanā:
(lo, i) It is precisely through the connection of these objects—which are incompatible with bathing in a pond—that the mere absence of bathing in a pond [is established].

Because there was no sprouting, the phrase "you have not gone near him" implies by means of *viparīta-lakṣaṇā* (contrary indication) that "you have indeed gone"; here, the word "with him" (*tena saha*) is to be supplied before the verb "to go.
An example of [indication] characterized by the excellence of proximity to another is as follows:
“Behold, the crane shines motionless and still upon the lotus leaf, like a gem set within a vessel of pure emerald.”
"Like a conch-shell cord."
Here, by the stillness of the crane, its trustfulness is indicated;
by that, the solitude of this place is shown;
therefore, "this is the meeting-place"—thus is it said by someone to a secret lover standing nearby.
In this very context, the purpose is the excellence of the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgyārtha*), consisting in the solitude of the location.
*Vijñapriyā*:
This is the speech of a female messenger (*dūtī*) who is leading the suitor (*upanāyaka*) to a place of assignation; [the word] "ua" [expresses this].
The meaning is "you should know," which is equivalent to "behold.
"Niścala" is a vocative; or alternatively, "niścalaniṣpanda" may be taken as a single compound word.
Then, "even from the motionless" means from that which is devoid of movement;
"conch-shell" refers to a fragment of a conch.
By the proximity of the hero who is being addressed—the meaning is that the indication of the place of rendezvous is understood by the members of the assembly through suggestion (vyañjanā).
And likewise, regarding the phrase "it is manifested" (*dyotyate*), the ellipsis is that the manifestation is understood by the audience through suggestion (*vyañjanā*).
However, for the hero, the place of the appointment is understood through suggestion because of its difference from the speaker’s [direct] indication of the crane.
— *Locanā*:
(lo, ī) Regarding that which is constant (*nicca*): behold, the crane sits motionless and still upon the lotus leaf,
shining like a conch-shell or mother-of-pearl resting in a vessel of pure emerald.
"Niścali" means "devoid of effort"; this is an address to a *viṭa* (libertine).
A conch-shell is a *śaṅkha-śukti*.
A broken or harsh throat-sound is designated as *kāku* (a change in tone).
The varieties of *kāku* of the type described above are to be understood from the authoritative sources (*ākara*).
Locanā:
"(Lo, u) *Bhinna*—varieties; that is, varieties consisting of differences in respective auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*) up to differences in essential nature (*svarūpa*)."
Regarding this distinction, for example:
"Alas, intent on going to a most distant land because he is dependent upon his guru,
O friend, he will not return to this place made lovely by swarms of bees and cuckoos."
At the time of the fragrant [incense], he [should do so].
The rhetorical question "He will not come here;
rather, he will surely come" is suggested through the use of intonation (*kāku*).—
*Vijñapriyā*:
Regarding "from the sources": the *ākara* (source) refers to a treatise that analyzes *kāku* (intonation), such as [the work] beginning with "a voice distinct from the natural throat-sound.
The meaning is that it is a throat-sound different from the natural (*svābhāvika*) throat-sound.
Regarding "due to dependence on the teacher": this is the statement of the first half [of the verse], spoken by a heroine grieving for her husband who has gone to a very distant land.
The second half of the verse is the speech of the friend who is consoling her.

Regarding the phrase "he will not come"—the meaning is "on the contrary, he will certainly come," which is suggested by means of *kāku* (intonation). Through *kāku*, the sense of the negative particle (*na*) is brought to mind; thus, the form [of the utterance] is "he will not come" [in words], but "he will certainly come" [in meaning].
In this context, the distinctive feature of *kāku* is its arising simultaneously with the movement of the head.
An example of excellence in gesture (*ceṣṭā*) is as follows:

"Having perceived that the lover was thinking of the time for their tryst, the clever woman closed her playful lotus-eyes, which had conveyed a hidden intention through a glance from her smiling eyes."
Locanā:
"By *saṅketa*—meaning by one who has conveyed a hidden intention (*ākūta*) through a laughing, blossoming eye"—this is an epithet of the *viṭa*.
Furthermore, as for the status of these aforementioned examples as *dhvani* or *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya*, this will become clear later in the detailed analysis thereof.
However, this is an illustration based solely on the fact that suggestion (*vyañjanā*) has a semantic function.

By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "gestures and so forth," there is the inclusion of the *sāttvika* and other states belonging to the hero (*nāyaka*) and others who are to be described.
Here, by means of gestures such as the closing of the eyes, it is suggested by a certain woman that "the twilight is the time for the secret meeting."
Vijñapriyā:

"(vi, ma) *saṃketakāle*—the meaning is: having perceived that the gallant (*viṭa*), the rogue (*dhūrta*), the lover (*upanāyaka*), was intent on the time for the rendezvous, and thus had his mind fixed upon it out of a desire to know [her intentions].
*Hasatā netreṇārpitam* means: in such a way that the playful lotus (*līlāpadma*) was closed, wherein an intention (*ākūta*) or state of being (*bhāva*) was conveyed by the smiling eye."
The meaning of "dyotyate" (is manifested) is that it is understood by the actor (*viṭa*);
however, it should be understood that the members of the audience also perceive that manifestation.
In this way, it should be understood that the distinction applies to the speaker and so forth, both individually and collectively.
This threefold nature of meanings is considered to be threefold for each [of the aforementioned factors]. (VisSd 2.17)

"Since meanings possess three forms—namely, the denoted (*vācya*), the indicated (*lakṣya*), and the suggested (*vyaṅgya*)—all the modes of suggestion (*vyañjanā*) mentioned immediately above are likewise of three kinds.
Among these, an example of the suggestion of the denoted meaning is: ‘The season is spring... and so forth.
An example of the suggestion of the indicated meaning is: ‘The sandalwood paste has been entirely washed away... and so forth."
As for the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgyārtha*), there is the example beginning with "ua ṇiccala-.
The manner in which verbal roots, suffixes, and so forth function as suggestors will be elaborated upon later.
A word understood through its own form suggests a meaning, while a word also depends upon another meaning [to suggest].
When one [cause] is the manifestor, the other becomes its auxiliary cause.
Locanā:

[The term] *śabdabodhya* (to be understood from the word) requires another meaning (*arthāntara*), and not merely that which conveys a single meaning (*ekārtha*), as in the case of [the expression] "surpassed by Durgā" (*durgālaṅghita*) and so forth.
The meaning also depends upon the word, as in cases such as "the time is spring" and so forth.
This is the meaning of the phrase "of one [of the two]" and so on:

when either the word or the meaning functions as the manifestor (*vyañjaka*), the other serves as its auxiliary (*sahakārī*); however, that [auxiliary] exists merely by virtue of its presence being unavoidable.
However, wherever a particular power is predominant, there the designation "suggestive" (vyañjaka) is based upon that;
for even in the case of suggestiveness, a word requires another element [in the form of] meaning,
and meaning likewise requires a word.
Therefore, when one [word] acts as a manifestor, it must necessarily be admitted that another serves as its auxiliary cause.

Due to being characterized by the three limiting conditions (*upādhi*) such as denotation (*abhidhā*) and so forth, the word is considered to be of three kinds: likewise, it is a denoter (*vācaka*), an indicator (*lakṣaka*), and a suggestor (*vyañjaka*). (ViSd 2.19)
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, ya) Due to the tenfold distinction of the speaker, the person to be addressed, and so forth, the meaning expressed through suggestion is threefold because of the three types of suggestive meanings; thus he says—“of the meanings,” that is, of the suggestive meanings.
This tenfold suggestion (*vyañjanā*)—

in the passage beginning with "without remainder" (*niḥśeṣa*) and so forth— the capacity of the indicated meaning (*lakṣyārtha*) to suggest has been stated solely according to his own philosophical view, because he has already explained the threefold nature of the suggestive word and meaning. Now, he states that the suggestive word (*vyañjaka-śabda*) is also threefold, [beginning with] the words "the triad of denotation and so forth" (*abhidhāditraya*).
That which has the conventional designation (*abhidhā*) as its limiting condition is the denoter (*vācaka*);
that which has the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) as its limiting condition is the indicator (*lakṣaka*);
and that which has the manifestation (*vyañjana*) as its limiting condition is the manifester (*vyañjaka*).
Furthermore:
Others say there is a function called *tātparya* (intentional import) for the purpose of cognizing the connection between word-meanings;
they hold that the meaning of this [function] is the intentional import (*tātparyārtha*), and that the sentence is the means of cognizing it. (VisSd 2.20)
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, ra) Not only are the three types [of meaning] such as the denoted (*vācya*) the meaning of a word, but even the relation between word-meanings (*padārthasaṃsarga*), which is distinct from the triad beginning with the denoted, is also the meaning of a word; and it is the sentence that conveys this. Thus he says, starting with "Furthermore" (*kiṃ ca*).
Regarding the comprehension of the relation between word-meanings,
other Naiyāyikas maintain that there is a function (vṛtti) called *tātparya* (intentional import) which serves as the cause for that comprehension of the relation.

For that purpose, they state that the object of this function— the meaning consisting of the relation— is the *tātparyārtha* (the intentional meaning), and that the sentence is the indicator of that [relation].

According to the proponents of the theory that meaning is conveyed by words once uttered (*abhihitānvayavādins*), there exists a function called *tātparya* (intentional import) which conveys the connection between word-meanings—that is, the sentence-meaning—since the denotative function (*abhidhā*) ceases after conveying the meaning of each individual word. The object of this [function] is the *tātparyārtha* (the intentional meaning), and the sentence is that which conveys it; such is their view.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, la) Demonstrating that denotation (*abhidhā*) lacks the capacity to bring about the cognition of a relation (*saṃsarga*), he explains [the verse] with the words "of denotation" (*abhidhāyāḥ*).
And "that object" (*tadarthaḥ*) means having the form of a relation (*saṃsargarūpa*).

For the Naiyāyikas, who maintain the theory that the meaning is conveyed by the words (abhihitānvaya-vāda), once the word-meaning has been denoted and recalled by the word, the cognition of its syntactic relation arises from the sentence alone.
Thus ends the commentary on the second chapter of the *Sāhityadarpaṇa-ṭīkā*.
Here concludes the second chapter of the *Sāhityadarpaṇa*, titled "The Definition of the Nature of the Sentence."
